title: feat(protocol): support CreateContractV2HostFn invocations
description: Handle `SOROBAN_AUTHORIZED_FUNCTION_TYPE_CREATE_CONTRACT_V2_HOST_FN` everywhere the library reads an invocation tree: `Inspect`, `Verify`, `DiffEntries`, the risk analyzer and the tree renderer.
why: `CreateContractV2HostFn` carries constructor arguments, which a V1 create does not. Today the create arm is handled generically — `diff.go` byte-compares it rather than reading its fields, and `Inspect` reports no constructor detail — so an entry that authorizes a contract deployment with attacker-chosen constructor args looks the same as a harmless one.
criteria: `Inspect` reports the wasm hash, salt and constructor argument count for both create arms.
`DiffEntries` reports a changed wasm hash, salt or constructor argument at its own path rather than as one opaque difference.
The risk analyzer treats a create-with-constructor-args as a distinct finding from a plain create.
A golden vector covers a V2 create with at least two constructor arguments, generated by the pinned JS SDK.
guidance: Read the arm's fields from `go-stellar-sdk`'s `xdr` package rather than assuming the field names; cite the file you read.
`diff.go`'s `diffInvocation` has a `default:` branch that byte-compares non-contract-fn arms — that is the seam to extend.
Do not change what is signed. The preimage already covers the whole invocation tree; this is reporting only.

title: feat(protocol): helpers for the Stellar Asset Contract admin interface (CAP-46-6)
description: Add helpers that build and recognise authorization entries for the SAC admin functions — `set_admin`, `set_authorized`, `clawback`, `mint` — so a caller signing one knows which it is.
why: SAC admin calls are the highest-consequence authorizations a classic asset issuer makes, and today they are indistinguishable from any other `contract_fn` entry. `clawback` and `set_admin` in particular are irreversible.
criteria: A recogniser that, given an entry, reports whether its root invocation is a SAC admin call and which one.
`Inspect` surfaces that classification in a new field, empty for non-SAC entries.
The risk analyzer flags `set_admin` and `clawback` at its highest severity, with a test asserting the severity and not merely that something was flagged.
Recognition is by function name and argument shape, with a test proving a same-named function on a non-SAC contract is not misreported.
guidance: Cite CAP-46-6 for each function's name and argument list; do not work from memory.
A contract address alone cannot prove a contract is a SAC, and claiming otherwise offline would be dishonest — report the shape match and say what it does not establish.
`risk.go` already has a severity scheme; reuse it rather than adding a second one.

title: feat(protocol): parse simulateTransaction responses into entries and resources
description: A typed reader that turns a `SimulateTransactionResponse` into the authorization entries it recorded, the resource footprint, the minimum resource fee, and the auth mode the host actually used.
why: `rpcflow.SignAndSubmit` does this inline. Every caller who wants the two-pass flow without that helper's opinions reimplements the parsing, and the subtle part — which arm the host recorded, and whether `UseUpgradedAuth` was honoured — is exactly what gets guessed wrong.
criteria: Returns the entries, the `SorobanTransactionData`, the minimum resource fee, and the observed credential arm per entry.
Reports whether the response is a recording or enforcing result rather than requiring the caller to remember which pass they ran.
A simulation error, or a response with no auth and no result, is an error naming which field was missing — never an empty success.
Offline tests drive it from committed JSON response fixtures, so the suite stays network-free.
guidance: Live in `rpcflow`, and refactor `SignAndSubmit` onto it so there is one parser, not two.
Capture the fixtures from a real testnet simulation and commit them; say in the PR which ledger and RPC version they came from.
Read `protocols/rpc/simulate_transaction.go` in the pinned SDK for the response shape and cite line numbers.

title: feat(protocol): compute the resource-fee delta signatures add
description: Given an unsigned entry and the signature shape that will fill it, estimate the increase in XDR size and the resource fee it implies — before the signer is called.
why: The two-pass simulation requirement exists because signatures cost resources. A caller who wants to know whether the enforcing pass will blow a fee ceiling currently finds out only after the signers have approved, which for a hardware wallet or a multi-party flow is the expensive moment to discover it.
criteria: Reports the byte delta exactly (it is computable: the signature `ScVal`'s marshalled length) and the fee delta as a documented function of it.
Handles the delegates arm, where every node's signature counts.
Any part of the fee that depends on a network setting the library cannot know offline is reported as such rather than guessed.
A test compares the predicted byte delta against a real signed entry's actual size and asserts they agree exactly.
guidance: Be precise about which half is exact and which is an estimate; a confident wrong fee is worse than no fee.
Cite the fee rule from the protocol or the host rather than deriving it from one observation.
An e2e assertion against a real enforcing-pass fee would make this evidence rather than arithmetic.

title: feat(protocol): contract addresses as delegates
description: Audit and complete support for a `C…` contract address appearing as a delegate at any depth: ordering, validation, signing, verification and reporting.
why: CAP-71-01 permits a contract as a delegate — that is how a smart account delegates to another smart account — but every fixture and golden vector uses `G…` delegates. The ordering comparison, the `cannot_check` path and the tree renderer are all untested against a contract delegate, so whether they are correct is currently unknown rather than known.
criteria: Golden vectors covering a contract delegate, a contract delegate nested under a G-account delegate, and a mixed level that exercises the XDR byte ordering between the two address types.
`VerifyEntry` reports a contract delegate as `cannot_check` with a reason naming the contract, never as `unsigned`.
An e2e scenario on testnet where a smart account delegates to another smart account.
A test asserting the ordering of a mixed `G…`/`C…` level matches what the pinned JS SDK produces.
guidance: `ScAddress` discriminates account before contract, so the byte ordering between the two types is decided by the discriminant — prove this with the SDK rather than asserting it.
`e2e/contracts/modular-account` is the natural delegate target; a second instance of it can be the delegating account.
If any current behaviour turns out wrong, that fix is its own commit with the evidence that found it.

title: feat(protocol): reconstruct the __check_auth Context a host would pass
description: Build the `Vec<Context>` an account contract's `__check_auth` receives for a given entry, so a caller can reason about — and a test can assert — what the contract will actually see.
why: An account contract's policy is written against the contexts it is handed, not against the entry. Today the only way to learn what those contexts are is to deploy the contract and simulate, which makes policy bugs a testnet-only discovery.
criteria: Produces the contexts for a contract-fn root with sub-invocations, and for both create arms.
The mapping from invocation tree to contexts is cited to the protocol or `rs-soroban-env`, not inferred from one example.
An e2e test compares the reconstruction against what a fixture contract actually receives, logging both.
Where the reconstruction cannot be exact offline, it reports that rather than returning a plausible guess.
guidance: This is a correctness claim about host behaviour, so it needs the host source: name the file and function.
A fixture contract that echoes its contexts in a diagnostic event would make the e2e comparison direct.
Fail closed: an invocation shape the mapping does not cover is an error, not a partial context list.

title: feat(protocol): golden vectors covering every ScVal argument type
description: Extend the generator so the invocation arguments in the vector set cover every `ScVal` type the XDR defines, including the nested and edge-case ones.
why: The vectors prove byte equality against the JS SDK for the argument types they happen to use. A type nobody put in a vector — `ScvI256`, `ScvDuration`, a deeply nested map, an empty vec — is untested, and the XDR encoding of exactly those is where a cross-implementation disagreement would hide.
criteria: A vector whose argument list includes every `ScValType` the pinned SDK can construct, with the ones it cannot documented and listed.
Boundary values for each numeric type: zero, minimum, maximum.
The differential and parity harnesses pick the new vectors up without changes, or the PR explains why they cannot.
`make vectors-check` stays green, and no committed vector is hand-edited.
guidance: `testdata/gen/gen.mjs` is the only place these are built; the generator refuses any SDK version but the pin.
Enumerate the types from the XDR definition rather than from memory, and say where you read it.
If a type turns out to disagree across implementations, stop and report it — do not adjust a vector to make a test pass.

title: feat(protocol): entries across a multi-operation transaction
description: Handle a transaction carrying several `invokeHostFunction` operations, each with its own authorization entries: signing them as one batch, reporting them with their operation index, and reassembling them in place.
why: `EnvelopeEntries` and `InspectEnvelope` read entries out of an envelope, but the write path back — signing a whole envelope's worth of entries and putting each back where it came from — does not exist. A caller with a two-operation transaction has to do that bookkeeping by hand, and putting an entry back on the wrong operation produces a transaction that pays fees and fails.
criteria: A function that takes an envelope and signers and returns an envelope with every address entry signed, preserving operation and entry order exactly.
An entry with no applicable signer fails the whole call naming its operation and entry index, never a partial envelope.
A test proving the input envelope's bytes are unchanged, and a test proving a round trip through read-and-write with no signers is byte-identical.
Fee-bump envelopes are read through to the inner transaction, with a test.
guidance: `envelope.go` already has the read side; this is its counterpart, and the two should share one notion of position.
`txnbuild.Transaction` has no exported fields and `GetInvokeHostFunctionOp()` returns a copy — work at the `xdr` level, not through `txnbuild`.
All-or-nothing, like `AuthorizeAll`: never return a half-signed envelope with a non-nil error.

title: feat(protocol): detect and refuse nonce reuse across a batch
description: Refuse a batch in which two address entries for the same address carry the same nonce, and surface the check for callers assembling entries from several sources.
why: The host consumes a nonce per address so an entry cannot be replayed. Two entries in one transaction sharing an address and a nonce means the second is rejected during application, after fees — and the failure reads as an authorization problem rather than the bookkeeping mistake it is. `noncetracker.go` tracks nonces a caller issued; it does not catch a collision in a batch assembled from elsewhere.
criteria: `AuthorizeAll` refuses such a batch with a sentinel error naming the address, both entry indices and the nonce.
An exported check callable independently of signing, so a caller can validate before involving signers.
The same address with different nonces, and different addresses with the same nonce, both pass — with tests for each, since only the first pair is a conflict.
The new sentinel has a test producing it, as `TestEverySentinelHasAProducingTest` requires.
guidance: Cite `verify_and_consume_nonce` for the host's rule rather than describing it from memory.
Check before any signer runs, so a hardware wallet is never asked to approve a batch that cannot land.
Source-account entries carry no nonce and must be skipped, not treated as a collision on the zero value.

title: feat(protocol): CAP-85 and Protocol 28 support once the Go SDK ships helpers
description: Re-audit the library against CAP-85 / Protocol 28 when `go-stellar-sdk` releases types and helpers for it, and either state that nothing changed or ship the change with a vector.
why: The README's CAP-85 section currently states, with evidence, that no change is required against SDK v0.7.3 — and commits to revisiting it when the SDK ships P28 helpers. That promise is only kept if someone does the audit.
criteria: The audit is recorded: which SDK version, which types are new, and whether any touches `SorobanAuthorizationEntry`, `SorobanCredentials`, `SorobanDelegateSignature` or the preimage variants.
If the wire format changed, a golden vector and an e2e scenario land with the change.
If nothing changed, the README section says so explicitly against the new version rather than being left stale.
`docs/sdk-support.md` records the version move under its existing policy.
guidance: Blocked until the SDK ships P28 helpers — check before starting, and say on the issue what you found.
Every claim here needs the file and line you read in the new SDK, not a release note summary.
If the audit finds nothing, that is a real and useful result; say it plainly.

title: feat(api): simulate an account contract's policy offline
description: Given an entry and a description of an account's policy — required signers, thresholds, which delegates must sign — report whether the entry as it stands satisfies it.
why: `AuthorizeAll` deliberately cannot know an account's policy, so it enforces only that nothing is wholly unsigned, and the docs tell callers to check the per-node `Signed` flags themselves. Everyone writes that check, and the delegates arm makes it non-obvious enough to get wrong.
criteria: A policy type expressive enough for the shipped fixture contracts: threshold-of-N delegates, a required signer, and nested requirements.
Reports which requirement is unmet and at which node, not a bare boolean.
Tests drive it from the fixture contracts' actual rules, so the model is checked against something real rather than invented.
The doc comment states plainly that this evaluates a policy the caller supplied and is not evidence about the deployed contract.
guidance: The honesty boundary is the whole value: a pass here must never read as a promise the transaction will succeed.
`threshold.go` and the fixture contracts in `e2e/contracts/` are the source for what policies look like in practice.
Fail closed on a policy the evaluator cannot express, rather than approximating it.

title: feat(api): streaming signer for very large delegate trees
description: Sign a delegate tree without materialising every node, so memory stays flat as the tree grows, and allow a caller to supply signatures lazily as they arrive.
why: `credentialNodes` walks the whole tree into a slice and `batch_sign.go` works from that. For the trees shipped today that is fine; for a tree assembled from many parties over time it means holding everything, and it forces every signature to exist before any is written.
criteria: A callback or iterator API that visits each node once, in a documented order, and writes a signature as it is produced.
A benchmark showing allocations flat as node count grows, compared against the current path.
Identical output bytes to the existing API for every golden vector — proven by test, not by inspection.
Cancellation is honoured mid-walk, with the entry left untouched rather than partly written.
guidance: The existing API stays; this is an addition for callers who need it, not a replacement.
`internal/xdrcopy` pools buffers — reuse that rather than adding a second pooling scheme.
The partial-write failure mode is the risk: a cancelled walk must not return a half-signed entry with a non-nil error.

title: feat(api): canonical JSON representation of an entry
description: A documented, stable JSON encoding of a `SorobanAuthorizationEntry` that round-trips to identical XDR bytes.
why: Entries move between tools as base64, which is exact and unreadable. `Inspect` is readable and lossy. There is nothing in between, so anything that needs to diff, review, store or template an entry invents its own lossy JSON.
criteria: Round-trips every golden vector to byte-identical XDR, asserted for all of them.
A schema document, and a version field so a later change is detectable rather than silent.
Rejects input it cannot represent exactly, rather than dropping a field.
Fuzz target asserting XDR → JSON → XDR is the identity.
guidance: Exactness is the whole point; a convenient encoding that loses a field is worse than none.
Reuse the decode-depth bound — this is another untrusted-input surface.
Coordinate with the differential harness: a canonical JSON would make cross-implementation cases easier to write.

title: feat(api): templating entries for repeated authorizations
description: Build an entry from a template plus the fields that change per submission — nonce, expiration, and chosen arguments — with validation that nothing else moved.
why: A backend authorizing the same call repeatedly rebuilds the whole entry each time, and the risk is a field drifting unnoticed between submissions. A template makes the invariant part explicit and checkable.
criteria: A template type that pins the invocation tree and address, and requires nonce and expiration per instantiation.
A checker that, given a template and an entry, reports whether the entry is an instance of it and what differs if not.
Reuses `DiffEntries` for the comparison rather than reimplementing structural equality.
A test proving two instantiations differing only in nonce produce different payloads.
guidance: `DiffEntries` already separates payload-affecting fields from the rest; a template is the same distinction applied forward.
Nonce generation stays in `invocation.go` — do not add a second source of randomness.
Never let a template carry a signature: the payload changes per instance, so a stored signature would be invalid by construction.

title: feat(api): typed accessors for the credentials union
description: Replace the repeated `switch entry.Credentials.Type` blocks with one typed accessor layer that makes an unhandled arm a compile-time or single-point failure instead of a copy of the same switch.
why: `arm.go` introduced an arm abstraction, but the switch on `Credentials.Type` still appears across `inspect.go`, `verify.go`, `diff.go`, `batch.go` and `upgrade.go`. Adding a fifth credential arm means finding every one of them, and the cost of missing one is a silent wrong answer rather than an error.
criteria: One place that maps a credentials value to its arm behaviour, with every caller going through it.
A test that fails if a new `SorobanCredentialsType` is handled in fewer places than it should be — a registry check, not a comment asking people to remember.
No change to any exported signature, and no change to any golden vector's bytes.
`go test -race ./...` and every parity suite stay green, proving the refactor is behaviour-preserving.
guidance: `arm.go` is the existing seam; extend it rather than introducing a parallel abstraction.
Behaviour-preserving means byte-identical: the vectors are the proof, so run them before and after.
`refactor: scaffolding for future credential arms` from Wave 9 is the groundwork — read what it did first.

title: feat(api): structured audit record for every signing decision
description: An optional recorder that captures, per signing call, what was signed: arm, address, nonce, expiration, payload hash, target node, and the decision taken — in a form suitable for an append-only log.
why: `hooks.go` emits events for metrics and tracing, which is the right shape for observability and the wrong shape for an audit trail: events are sampled, unordered and droppable. An operator asked to prove which payloads their service signed has nothing to hand over.
criteria: A record type carrying the payload hash and every preimage-derived field, with a stable serialisation.
Records are produced for refusals too — a refused signature is the most interesting line in an audit log.
No secret, seed or signature value is ever recorded; a test asserts the record contains none.
Documented ordering and delivery guarantees, including what happens when the sink fails.
guidance: Build on `hooks.go` only if its guarantees can be stated honestly; otherwise keep audit separate and say why in the doc comment.
The library does no logging — this hands records to a caller-supplied sink, it does not write files.
A sink that errors must not silently drop a record; decide and document whether that fails the signing call.

title: feat(api): entry expiry and freshness policy helpers
description: Helpers that answer, for an entry and a current ledger, whether it is still valid, how many ledgers remain, and whether it is inside a caller-chosen safety margin.
why: `ExpirationAfter` computes an expiration going in. Nothing reads one back out. A service holding pre-signed entries has to re-derive the inclusive-bound rule itself every time, and that rule is exactly the one the JS SDK documents the other way round.
criteria: A validity check implementing the host's inclusive bound, cited to `verify_and_consume_nonce`.
Remaining-ledger count, and a margin check for a caller-supplied threshold.
Handles the delegates arm, where the top-level expiration governs every node.
A table test covering the boundary ledgers either side, since off-by-one is the whole risk.
guidance: `expiration.go` is the home; keep the existing doc-comment table as the single statement of the rule.
The network's `max_live_until_ledger` is not knowable offline — do not cap, and say so.
A source-account entry has no expiration; return an error rather than a misleading `true`.

title: feat(api): merge independently signed copies of one entry
description: Combine several copies of the same entry, each signed by a different party, into one fully signed entry — refusing any pair that does not agree on the payload.
why: `coordinator.go` sequences multi-party signing, which assumes the parties take turns. Parties who sign in parallel each hold a copy, and merging them by hand is where a mismatched expiration silently invalidates the others' signatures.
criteria: Refuses to merge copies whose payload-affecting fields differ, naming the field and the two values.
Refuses two different signatures for the same node unless the caller explicitly chooses one.
The merged entry is byte-identical to the same signatures applied sequentially, asserted against a golden vector.
Reuses `DiffEntries` for the agreement check rather than reimplementing it.
guidance: The refusal is the feature. A merge that quietly picks a winner produces an entry that looks complete and fails on-chain.
`docs/multi-party-signing.md` states why the expiration must be fixed before anyone signs — this is the parallel case of that rule.
All-or-nothing: on any disagreement return no entry, not a partial merge.

title: feat(api): pluggable signature-shape registry
description: Let a caller register a custom account's signature shape so `DescribeSignature`, `VerifyEntry` and the risk analyzer can recognise and check it instead of reporting `cannot_check`.
why: `cannot_check` is the honest answer for a shape the library does not know, and it is also a dead end: a wallet vendor who knows their own shape has no way to teach it to the library, so their users get no verification at all.
criteria: A registry taking a shape matcher and a verifier, with the built-in ed25519 and passkey shapes registered through the same mechanism.
A registered verifier that fails reports `invalid`, never `cannot_check` — the distinction `VerifyVerdict` exists for.
A registered shape cannot cause a false `verified`: a test asserts a verifier returning success on wrong bytes is still reported honestly, or that this is impossible by construction.
Registration is explicit and per-caller; no global mutable default, and a test proving concurrent use is safe.
guidance: `verify.go`'s four verdicts already carry the right distinctions — extend their sources, not the verdict set.
The trust boundary needs stating: a registered verifier is the caller's claim, not the library's, and the report should make that legible.
`SignerFunc` is the existing escape hatch on the signing side; this is its counterpart on the reading side.

title: feat(api): deterministic test-entry builders for downstream test suites
description: An exported, documented builder package producing entries of every arm with fixed addresses, nonces and invocation trees, for use in other projects' tests.
why: The in-repo fixtures (`entryForArm`, `delegatesFixture`) are unexported test helpers, so every downstream project writing tests against soroauth hand-builds XDR structs — and a wrong fixture makes their tests pass for the wrong reason.
criteria: Builders for all four arms plus a nested delegate tree, deterministic across runs and platforms.
Keys derived by the repo's documented label scheme, with the package stating plainly that they are public test keys and must never be funded on mainnet.
The repo's own tests are refactored onto it, so it cannot drift from what is actually used.
Importing it pulls in no test-only dependency and no `testing` import in non-test files.
guidance: A separate importable package, not the root — a test helper in the root package surface invites production use.
`docs` already documents the deterministic key scheme; cite it rather than restating the derivation.
If exporting the existing helpers verbatim would freeze an awkward signature, design the API first and migrate the tests onto it.

title: feat(signers): Azure Key Vault signer
description: A `Signer` backed by Azure Key Vault / Managed HSM, in its own Go module under `adapters/azurekv`, matching the shape the AWS and GCP KMS adapters already set.
why: Azure is the third of the three clouds a backend is likely to already be on, and its absence is the reason an Azure-hosted service hand-rolls a signer. The adapter pattern is established; this is filling the gap in it.
criteria: Its own `go.mod`, so the root module gains no Azure dependency.
Produces the classic-account `ScVal` shape, verified against `NewEd25519Signer`'s output for the same key material where the key type allows it.
A typed-nil client is rejected rather than panicking, as `adapters/gcpkms` does via its `isNilClient` check.
Offline tests against a fake client covering success, permission failure and context cancellation; no test needs an Azure account.
guidance: Read `adapters/awskms` and `adapters/gcpkms` first and follow them; three adapters that differ in shape is worse than three that match.
Azure's Ed25519 support varies by tier — state plainly in the doc comment which key types are supported and which are refused.
`ci-adapters.yml` reads each adapter's own `go.mod` for its toolchain; add the job the same way.

title: feat(signers): PKCS#11 signer for HSMs and smartcards
description: A `Signer` speaking PKCS#11, in its own module, covering the YubiKey PIV and SoftHSM cases.
why: PKCS#11 is the one interface that covers every on-premise HSM and most smartcards at once, so a single adapter replaces a long tail of vendor-specific ones. It is also the only option for an operator who cannot use a cloud KMS.
criteria: Its own module; the root module gains no CGO dependency.
Session and PIN handling documented, with the PIN never accepted as a struct literal that could end up in a log — and a test asserting no error message contains it.
Tests run against SoftHSM in CI so the path is exercised without hardware.
A documented list of what was actually tested on real hardware, and what was not.
guidance: CGO is the reason this cannot live in the root module; say so in the doc comment.
Follow `docs/signers.md`'s threat-model framing and add this signer to its table.
Do not claim hardware support you have not run; `docs/signers.md` is explicit about evidence per signer.

title: feat(signers): Trezor hardware wallet signer
description: A `Signer` for Trezor devices, alongside the existing Ledger adapter, including the device-confirmation flow and its failure modes.
why: Ledger shipped in Wave 9 and Trezor is the other device a Stellar user is likely to hold. Without it, Trezor users are the one hardware cohort with no path through this library.
criteria: Device rejection, timeout and disconnection are distinct errors, not one opaque failure.
The preimage is passed to the device so the user confirms what they are approving, not a bare hash.
Offline tests against a fake transport cover each failure mode; a documented manual run against real hardware records firmware version and what was confirmed on screen.
`docs/signers.md` gains a row stating the evidence for this signer honestly.
guidance: Read the Ledger adapter first and match its ergonomics and error taxonomy.
`Signer.Sign` receives both preimage and payload precisely so a device signer can show the user the real thing — use it.
A hardware signer must never be asked to confirm something that will be discarded; the pre-sign guards in `authorize.go` already ensure this, so do not bypass them.

title: feat(signers): batched user presence for passkey and hardware signers
description: Let one user confirmation cover several entries, where the signer and the payload set allow it, instead of one prompt per entry.
why: A delegate tree or a multi-operation transaction needs several signatures. With a hardware or passkey signer that is one prompt each, which users click through without reading — the prompt stops being a security control precisely when there are most of them.
criteria: An API that presents the full set of payloads for one confirmation and then produces every signature.
Refuses to batch across differing addresses or expirations unless the caller explicitly opts in, since those are different authorizations.
A test proving the batched result is byte-identical to signing each entry individually.
The doc comment states what the user is actually confirming, and what is lost compared with per-entry prompts.
guidance: The honesty question matters more than the ergonomics: one prompt for twenty payloads must not read as one authorization.
`batch_sign.go` is the existing batch path; extend it rather than adding a parallel one.
Not every signer can do this — make it an optional interface a signer may implement, with a documented fallback.

title: feat(signers): key rotation and versioned signer identity
description: Support a signer whose underlying key can change — a rotated KMS key version — while the account address stays the same, including which version signed a given entry.
why: Every KMS adapter signs with whatever version the key alias currently points at. After a rotation, an entry signed before it and an entry signed after are indistinguishable, so an operator investigating a bad signature cannot tell which key produced it.
criteria: A signer may report the key version it used, and that version reaches the audit record and the hook events.
A rotation mid-batch is detected and refused rather than producing a batch signed by two keys without saying so.
Tests against a fake KMS covering rotation between two calls.
`docs/signers.md` states what rotation means for entries already signed and not yet submitted.
guidance: `Signer.Address()` is the account identity and must not change on rotation — the version is extra, not a replacement.
For a classic account the public key is in the signature itself, so a rotation that changes it changes who can authorize: state that consequence plainly.
Coordinate with the audit-record issue so there is one notion of key version, not two.

title: feat(signers): rate-limited and quota-aware signer wrapper
description: A decorator that bounds how often a wrapped signer is called, with the limit, the wait behaviour and the refusal all explicit.
why: A cloud KMS bills per operation and throttles; a compromised service that can call a signer without bound can drain a quota or sign an unbounded number of authorizations before anyone notices. Rate limiting is a containment control and there is nowhere to put it today.
criteria: A documented limiter whose refusal is a distinct error a caller can match on, not a generic failure.
Context cancellation and deadline are honoured while waiting, with a test asserting the wrapped signer was not called.
Concurrency-safe, with a `-race` test driving it from several goroutines.
Composes with the retry wrapper from Wave 9 in both orders, with the recommended order documented and justified.
guidance: Follow the existing retry/backoff wrapper's shape so the decorators are recognisably a family.
No `math/rand`: if jitter is wanted, use `crypto/rand`, per the repo's coding standards.
Waiting silently is the wrong default for a signing path — make blocking versus refusing an explicit choice.

title: feat(signers): policy-enforcing signer wrapper
description: A decorator that inspects what it is about to sign and refuses if it violates caller-supplied rules — contract allowlist, maximum amount argument, forbidden SAC admin calls.
why: The last place a bad authorization can be stopped is the signer, and it is the only place that sees every one. `SignerFunc` lets a caller write this by hand against raw XDR, which is the error-prone way to do a security check.
criteria: Rules evaluated against the decoded invocation tree, not the raw bytes, and reusing the risk analyzer where it already answers the question.
A refusal names the rule and the offending node; it is a distinct error type.
Fails closed: a tree the rules cannot evaluate is refused, not allowed, with a test proving it.
A test proving the wrapped signer is never invoked on a refusal.
guidance: `risk.go` already classifies entries — build on it so there is one set of heuristics with one set of documented limits.
`docs/analyzer-heuristics.md` states what the analyzer misses; the wrapper's doc comment must inherit those caveats rather than implying completeness.
An allowlist is a real control; an amount check on an arbitrary ScVal argument is heuristic. Do not present the second as the first.

title: feat(signers): Turnkey signer
description: A `Signer` backed by Turnkey's signing API, in its own module.
why: Turnkey is a key-management service several Stellar wallet teams already use, and its policy engine pairs naturally with the authorization entries this library builds. Today those teams write a bespoke `SignerFunc`.
criteria: Its own module; no root-module dependency.
Request signing and credential handling follow the vendor's documented scheme, cited.
Offline tests against a recorded HTTP transport covering success, a policy denial and cancellation.
A policy denial from the service is a distinct, matchable error, since it is an expected outcome rather than a fault.
guidance: `remote/` already defines a signing protocol and reference server — if the vendor's API maps onto it, reuse rather than duplicate.
Never commit a credential or a recorded response containing one; scrub the fixtures and say in the PR how.
State in the doc comment what is proven by test and what was only run by hand.

title: feat(signers): Fireblocks signer
description: A `Signer` backed by Fireblocks' raw-signing API, in its own module, including the asynchronous approval flow.
why: Fireblocks is the custody platform institutional Stellar holders use, and its signing is asynchronous with human approval — a flow the current `Signer` interface has never been exercised against. Supporting it tests whether the interface is actually sufficient.
criteria: The asynchronous approval is handled within the `Signer` contract, or the PR states precisely why the interface is insufficient and what minimal change it needs.
Long waits are bounded by the context, with a test asserting cancellation does not leak a goroutine.
Offline tests against a recorded transport covering approval, rejection and timeout.
A rejection by a human approver is a distinct error, not a timeout.
guidance: If the interface genuinely does not fit, say so on the issue before building a workaround — that finding is more valuable than the adapter.
`feat(signers): cancellation and deadline semantics audit` from Wave 9 set the rules here; read it and comply.
Scrub every recorded fixture of credentials and account identifiers.

title: feat(signers): threshold signing with real key shares
description: Complete the threshold/MPC signer interface from Wave 9 with a working Ed25519 threshold implementation, or document with evidence why it cannot be done safely in-repo.
why: Wave 9 shipped the interface; nothing implements it, so whether the interface is right is unknown. An unimplemented interface in a signing library is a liability — it reads as a supported capability.
criteria: Either a working implementation with test vectors, or a written finding explaining what blocks it and what the interface should become.
If implemented: the aggregated signature verifies under the standard Ed25519 verifier, asserted against `NewEd25519Signer` output for a reconstructed key.
If implemented: the share-handling threat model is stated, including what this does not protect against.
If not implemented: the interface is either removed or clearly marked as unimplemented, so it cannot be mistaken for a shipped feature.
guidance: Rolling threshold cryptography by hand is the wrong answer. Use a reviewed library or report that none fits, with evidence.
This repo is unaudited and says so; a cryptographic primitive added here inherits that and the docs must not overclaim.
Classic Stellar multisig already solves many real cases — `AccountMultiSigner` exists, so say where threshold signing adds something it does not.

title: feat(signers): conformance test suite every signer must pass
description: An exported suite that takes a `Signer` and asserts the contract: address stability, context handling, determinism where applicable, no mutation of inputs, and correct behaviour on refusal.
why: There are now a dozen signer implementations across several modules, each tested its own way. The `Signer` contract is stated in prose in `signer.go` and nowhere enforced, so a new adapter can satisfy the compiler and violate the contract.
criteria: The suite is importable by the adapter modules and run by each of their test suites.
Covers: `Address()` is stable across calls, a cancelled context is honoured without signing, the preimage argument is not mutated, and a failure returns no partial `ScVal`.
Every shipped signer passes, and the PR reports any that did not before being fixed.
The suite fails loudly if handed a nil signer, rather than passing vacuously.
guidance: Model it on how `errors_meta_test.go` turns a prose rule into a check that bites.
A conformance suite that no implementation fails is either perfect or not checking anything — report what it caught.
Deterministic signers and interactive ones differ; let the suite be told which contract applies rather than assuming.

title: feat(signers): signer that proves possession before use
description: A startup check that a configured signer actually controls the address it claims, by signing and verifying a throwaway payload before the service accepts traffic.
why: A misconfigured KMS key alias or a wrong account address produces a service that starts cleanly and fails every submission on-chain, after fees. The mismatch is cheap to detect at startup and expensive to detect in production.
criteria: A check that signs a payload which cannot be a real authorization, and verifies the result against the claimed address.
For a custom account where the library cannot verify offline, it reports `cannot_check` rather than passing — the distinction `VerifyEntry` already draws.
`soroauth doctor` runs it when a signer is configured.
A test proving a signer whose address does not match its key is caught.
guidance: The throwaway payload must be unmistakably not an entry preimage; say in the doc comment why it cannot be replayed as one.
`doctor.go` is the natural home for the operator-facing half.
A pass here proves key control, not that the key is a signer of the account on-chain — state that limit.

title: feat(signers): WebAuthn attestation verification for passkey enrolment
description: Verify the attestation object produced when a passkey is created, so a wallet can check what authenticator a key came from before enrolling it as a signer.
why: `webauthn.go` parses assertions — the signing step. Enrolment is the other half, and it is where a wallet decides to trust a key at all. Without attestation checking, any claimed public key can be enrolled.
criteria: Parses the attestation object and verifies the statement for at least the `packed` and `none` formats, with unsupported formats refused rather than skipped.
Reports the authenticator AAGUID and whether the key is hardware-backed, clearly separating what was proven from what was merely asserted by the client.
Test vectors from a real authenticator or an established test library, committed, with their origin recorded.
A tampered attestation is rejected, with a test for each field that matters.
guidance: Cite the WebAuthn specification section for each check; this is a security verification and memory is not a source.
`none` attestation proves nothing about the authenticator — report it as such rather than as a weak pass.
Coordinate with `docs/passkeys.md` so enrolment and signing are described as one flow.

title: feat(signers): signer chain with explicit fallback and quorum
description: Combine several signers for one address under a declared rule — first that succeeds, or N of M must agree — with the rule and its failure modes explicit.
why: An operator with a primary KMS and a backup HSM currently writes the failover by hand, and the dangerous version is easy to write: fall through on any error, including a policy refusal that was meant to stop the signing.
criteria: A policy refusal is never treated as a transient failure to fall through from; a test proves it stops the chain.
For the quorum rule, disagreeing signatures are a refusal naming the signers, not a silent pick.
Every attempt reaches the audit record, including the ones that were skipped and why.
Context cancellation stops the chain immediately, with a test asserting no later signer was called.
guidance: The error taxonomy is the hard part: fallback is only safe when transient and terminal failures are distinguishable, so define that distinction first.
For a classic account, two different keys produce different signatures — a quorum here is not the same thing as `AccountMultiSigner`, so say which problem it solves.
Fail closed: an error the chain cannot classify is terminal.

title: feat(bindings): Python package wrapping the signing core
description: A published Python package exposing preimage construction, signing and inspection, built on the existing wasm core or a C shared library.
why: The Python `stellar-sdk` has the same gap the Go SDK had: no auth-entry signing helper. `testdata/parity-python` already proves the Python SDK can be driven to the same bytes, so the correctness groundwork exists and only packaging is missing.
criteria: Installable from a wheel with no Go toolchain required at install time.
Every golden vector replayed through the Python API in its CI, asserting byte equality.
The published API is documented, and its honesty boundaries match the Go library's — no verdict the Go library would call `cannot_check`.
Wheels built for Linux and macOS in CI, with the build reproducible from the repo.
guidance: `wasm/` and `cmd/soroauthwasm` already compile the core; reuse rather than starting a third surface.
`testdata/parity-python` has the pinned SDK and venv machinery — build on it.
A binding that can disagree with the Go library is worse than none, so the vector replay is the gate, not a nice-to-have.

title: feat(bindings): C shared library and header
description: A stable C ABI over the signing core, with a generated header, as the foundation other language bindings build on.
why: Each new binding currently needs its own path to the core. One reviewed C ABI makes Python, Ruby, PHP, Java and Swift bindings thin wrappers instead of separate reimplementations.
criteria: A documented ABI with explicit memory ownership rules and no Go pointers escaping into C.
Every error returned as a code plus a retrievable message; no path aborts the process.
Built for Linux, macOS and Windows in CI, with the golden vectors replayed through the C API on each platform.
An ASan or Valgrind run over the test harness, reported in the PR.
guidance: `c-shared` build mode plus `cgo` export comments is the mechanism; the hard part is ownership, so document it before writing it.
Secrets must not cross the boundary carelessly — define who zeroes what, and test it.
Keep the surface minimal: preimage, payload, sign, inspect, verify. Breadth can come later; a published ABI is hard to change.

title: feat(bindings): Java/JVM binding
description: A JVM library over the C ABI or the wasm core, published to a Maven repository.
why: Java is the dominant language in the custody and exchange systems that hold Stellar assets, and it is the ecosystem furthest from an auth-entry signing helper today.
criteria: Published artifact installable without a local Go or Rust toolchain.
Golden vectors replayed through the JVM API in CI with byte equality asserted.
Native libraries bundled for Linux and macOS, with the selection mechanism documented and tested.
Idiomatic exceptions carrying the same distinctions as the Go sentinels, so a caller can tell a refusal from a fault.
guidance: Depends on the C ABI issue; check its state before starting and say so on the issue.
Prefer the Foreign Function and Memory API over JNI if the baseline JDK allows it, and state the minimum version.
Mirror the Go library's honesty boundaries exactly; a JVM `verify` that returns a boolean would erase the `cannot_check` distinction.

title: feat(bindings): Rust crate over the signing core
description: A Rust crate exposing the same operations, for tooling that already depends on `stellar-xdr` and `soroban-sdk`.
why: The Soroban contract and tooling ecosystem is Rust, so Rust is where the consumers of these entries live. `testdata/parity-rust` already recomputes the vectors with the crate the host itself uses, which makes a native crate the shortest path from this library to that ecosystem.
criteria: Replays every golden vector with byte equality in CI.
Uses the same `stellar-xdr` version the parity harness pins, with the pin policy documented.
No `unsafe` outside a clearly justified and commented boundary.
Error types carry the same distinctions as the Go sentinels.
guidance: A native Rust implementation and a binding over the C ABI are different projects with different risks — pick one deliberately and say which on the issue.
If native: the parity harness becomes the correctness gate, so wire it in from the start.
`docs/parity.md` states what agreement across implementations does and does not establish; inherit that framing.

title: feat(integrations): Stellar Wallets Kit / Freighter integration
description: Wire the wasm package into Stellar Wallets Kit and Freighter so a browser dapp can sign an authorization entry through an installed wallet.
why: `examples/browser-passkey` proves the wasm core signs in a browser with a passkey. The far more common browser case is a user with Freighter installed, and that path does not exist, so dapps fall back to hand-rolled signing.
criteria: A working example signing an entry through a real wallet extension, with the flow documented end to end.
The signed entry is verified against the golden-vector path, so the wallet's output is checked and not assumed.
Wallet rejection, locked wallet and wrong-network are distinct, handled states in the example.
`docs/browser.md` gains the flow alongside the passkey one.
guidance: `adapters/walletsdk` and `wasm/ts` are the existing pieces; this connects them rather than adding a third.
A wallet that returns a signature for a different network must be caught — check the passphrase, do not trust the wallet to.
Say plainly in the docs which wallet versions were actually tested.

title: feat(integrations): gRPC signing and verification service
description: A gRPC surface over the operations the HTTP service already exposes, with a published protobuf schema.
why: `server/` and `remote/` speak HTTP/JSON. A backend fleet that standardises on gRPC either proxies or reimplements, and the protobuf schema is also the clearest machine-readable statement of the service contract.
criteria: A committed `.proto` with the schema, and generated code checked by CI to be in sync with it.
Parity tests asserting the gRPC and HTTP surfaces return equivalent results for the same inputs.
Deadlines and cancellation propagate to the signer, with a test.
The honesty boundaries of `verify` are preserved in the schema — `cannot_check` is a distinct value, not a false.
guidance: `remote/protocol.go` defines the existing contract; the proto should express the same thing, not a looser version.
This adds dependencies: keep it in its own module so the root module stays thin.
A service that signs needs its authentication story stated, not deferred — coordinate with the service-auth issue.

title: feat(integrations): GitHub Action to verify entries in a workflow
description: A published composite action wrapping `soroauth verify` and `soroauth inspect`, so a repository can gate on an entry's structure and signatures in CI.
why: Teams that commit or generate authorization entries have no way to check them in review. The CLI already does the work and exits with meaningful codes; what is missing is the packaging that makes it one line in a workflow.
criteria: Published and usable by SHA from another repository, with inputs for entry source, network and expected arm.
Findings surface as workflow annotations, not only as log text.
Its own integration test workflow in this repo, proving it fails on a bad entry and passes on a good one.
No secret is ever accepted as an action input, consistent with the CLI's rule.
guidance: Pin everything by commit SHA, as `CONTRIBUTING.md` requires of this repo's own workflows.
The container image from Wave 9 is the natural runtime — reuse it rather than installing Go in the action.
Add the action's own path to its workflow's `paths:` filter, or an edit to it will not run its own test.

title: feat(integrations): OpenAPI specification for the verification service
description: A committed OpenAPI document for the HTTP service, with CI asserting the implementation matches it.
why: `docs/verification-service.md` describes the service in prose. A client generator cannot read prose, and prose drifts from the handler without anything failing.
criteria: The spec covers every endpoint, status code and error shape the service actually returns.
A CI check that fails when the implementation and the spec disagree — a real conformance test, not a linter on the YAML.
A generated client is exercised against the running service in that check.
`docs/verification-service.md` links the spec rather than restating it.
guidance: Generate the check from the spec so drift is caught automatically; a hand-written parallel test will itself drift.
The `cannot_check` verdict must be representable — do not let the schema flatten it to a boolean.
Add the spec's path to the relevant workflow's `paths:` filter so editing it re-runs the check.

title: feat(integrations): harden the HTTP service for untrusted exposure
description: Add authentication, request size limits, timeouts, concurrency bounds and structured request logging to `server/`, and document the threat model it is then fit for.
why: `server/main.go` is a single file that accepts entries from anyone who can reach it and decodes them. The decode depth is bounded, which is the sharpest edge, but there is no auth, no body limit and no timeout — so it is only safe on a trusted network, and nothing says so.
criteria: Body size limit, read and write timeouts, and a bounded concurrent-request count, each configurable with a documented default.
An authentication mechanism, off by default only if the service refuses to bind a non-loopback address without it.
Request logs carry no entry bytes and no secret; a test asserts it.
`docs/verification-service.md` states the threat model, what is now safe, and what is still not.
guidance: The service verifies rather than signs today — if signing is ever added, the auth story becomes mandatory, so design for that now.
Refusing to start insecurely is better than a warning nobody reads; prefer fail-closed defaults.
An unbounded decode is the classic denial of service here; `MaxDecodeDepth` covers depth, so check size and count too.

title: feat(integrations): Prometheus metrics and a reference dashboard
description: Expose the hook events as Prometheus metrics from the service, and ship a Grafana dashboard definition for them.
why: `hooks.go` emits the events and `examples/opentelemetry` shows one consumer, but an operator running the service has nothing to look at. The signals that matter — refusal rate, signer latency, stale-signature findings — are exactly the ones that indicate something is wrong.
criteria: Metrics for request rate, verdict distribution, refusal reasons and signer latency, with documented names and labels.
No label carries an address, a nonce or anything else unbounded in cardinality; a test asserts the label sets are closed.
A committed dashboard JSON, with a screenshot or export proving it renders against real data.
The metrics endpoint is separable from the API port, so it need not be publicly exposed.
guidance: Build on `hooks.go` rather than instrumenting the handlers separately, so there is one event source.
High-cardinality labels are the usual way a metrics change takes down a Prometheus — hence the closed-label-set test.
The library itself does no logging and should gain no metrics dependency; this belongs in the service.

title: feat(integrations): multi-architecture signed container images
description: Publish the container image for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, signed and with an attached SBOM and provenance attestation.
why: Wave 9 publishes a single-architecture image. A consumer on arm64 — most recent laptops and much of current cloud capacity — cannot run it, and nothing about the published image is verifiable.
criteria: A manifest list covering both architectures, with both actually tested by running the CLI in CI.
Images signed, with the verification command documented so a consumer can check rather than trust.
An SBOM and a build provenance attestation attached to the published image.
The release workflow does all of this; no step is a documented manual ritual.
guidance: Reuse the existing release workflow and image build; this extends them rather than replacing them.
Keyless signing avoids a long-lived key in CI — if you choose otherwise, say why.
Document the verification command in the README; a signature nobody can check adds nothing.

title: feat(integrations): Homebrew tap and Nix flake for the CLI
description: Publish the CLI through a Homebrew tap and a Nix flake, both updated by the release workflow.
why: Installing the CLI means `go install` or downloading a release binary. The two package managers its likely users already have are the ones missing, and a hand-updated formula goes stale the first time nobody remembers.
criteria: Both install a working `soroauth` whose `--version` reports the released version, verified in CI on macOS and Linux.
The release workflow updates both automatically, including checksums.
The flake builds reproducibly and pins its inputs.
The README's install section covers both.
guidance: Automation is the point: a formula a human has to remember to bump is the thing being fixed.
The `--version` check in CI is what proves the package actually works, rather than merely building.
Reuse the release workflow's existing checksum generation rather than computing them twice.

title: feat(integrations): browser extension that explains an entry before signing
description: A reference extension that intercepts a signing request, renders the entry's structure and risk findings, and requires an explicit confirmation.
why: A browser user asked to sign an authorization entry sees base64. The library already has `Inspect`, the risk analyzer, the tree renderer and a wasm build — every piece needed to show the user what they are approving, with nothing assembling them at the point of decision.
criteria: Renders arm, address, nonce, expiration, the delegate tree and the invocation tree from the wasm core, not a reimplementation.
Risk findings are shown with the analyzer's documented limits visible, not as a safety verdict.
Works against the existing browser passkey example end to end.
States plainly that it reports structure and does not interpret what a contract call will do.
guidance: `soroauth-explain` is the project that interprets entries; this is the structural view, so link rather than duplicate it.
A reference extension, not a product: no store listing, no telemetry, no update channel.
`docs/analyzer-heuristics.md` lists what the analyzer misses — the UI must not imply more than that.

title: feat(integrations): Node.js native binding over the C ABI
description: A Node package exposing the signing core natively, for backends that cannot run the wasm build.
why: `@soroauth/wasm` targets the browser, and a Node backend pays wasm's startup and copying costs for no benefit. Node is also the most likely server-side consumer, since the reference implementation these vectors are proven against is the JS SDK.
criteria: Installs from a published package with prebuilt binaries, falling back to a source build.
Every golden vector replayed through the Node API in CI with byte equality asserted.
Prebuilds for Linux and macOS on the supported Node versions, with the matrix documented.
Errors surface as typed exceptions preserving the Go sentinels' distinctions.
guidance: Depends on the C ABI issue; check its state first and say so on the issue.
The wasm package stays — this is for Node, not a replacement, and the README should say which to use when.
A binding that can disagree with the Go library is worse than none, so the vector replay is the gate.

title: test: mutation testing over the signing path
description: Run a mutation tester over `preimage.go`, `authorize.go`, `delegates.go` and `diff.go`, and either kill every surviving mutant or record why it survives.
why: Coverage says these lines ran. It does not say a test would notice if they were wrong. For a library whose output moves money, the question that matters is whether a changed comparison or a flipped boundary is caught — and the only way to know is to change one and see.
criteria: A documented, reproducible way to run it locally, with a committed configuration.
Every surviving mutant is either killed by a new test or recorded with the reason it is equivalent or unreachable.
A report committed with the run's date, tool version and score.
At least one real test gap found and fixed, or a statement with evidence that none was.
guidance: Scope to the signing path first; mutation testing the whole repo will drown the signal.
Keep it out of required CI until the survivor list is empty — a noisy gate gets ignored.
A surviving mutant in the preimage builder is a finding worth its own commit, not a line in a report.

title: test: fuzz DiffEntries against entry pairs
description: A fuzz target feeding two decoded entries into `DiffEntries`, asserting its invariants rather than only that it does not panic.
why: `DiffEntries` landed with table tests. It walks two untrusted trees at once and makes a claim — `PayloadChanged` — that other code will act on, and nothing currently generates adversarial pairs.
criteria: Invariants asserted: a diff of an entry against itself is `Identical` with no changes; `PayloadChanged` is false whenever every preimage-derived field is equal; `StaleSignatures` is empty when `PayloadChanged` is false.
`PayloadChanged` is cross-checked against `Preimage`/`Payload` on both entries, so the fuzzer tests the claim and not the implementation's opinion of itself.
Seed corpus built from the golden vectors and their tampered variants, in `testdata/fuzz/`.
Wired into the continuous fuzzing workflow alongside the existing targets.
guidance: The payload cross-check is the valuable assertion — a fuzzer that only checks for panics would have missed every bug found while building the feature.
`cmd/gencorpus` already emits Go corpus format; extend it rather than hand-writing seeds.
Source-account entries have no payload; the invariant has to account for that rather than skipping them.

title: test: fuzz VerifyEntry
description: A fuzz target over `VerifyEntry`, asserting that it never reports `verified` for a signature that does not verify, and never panics on a malformed signature `ScVal`.
why: `VerifyEntry` decides whether a signature is good, and a false `verified` is the worst output this library can produce. Its tests use well-formed signatures; the inputs that would break it are the malformed ones.
criteria: A `verified` verdict is independently re-checked with `crypto/ed25519` in the target, so the verdict is validated and not assumed.
Malformed, truncated and wrong-type signature values produce a verdict, never a panic.
A node addressed to a contract is always `cannot_check`, asserted as an invariant.
Seed corpus from the vectors plus deliberately corrupted variants; wired into continuous fuzzing.
guidance: Independent re-verification is what makes this evidence rather than a tautology.
`docs/verification-limits.md` states the guarantees — the invariants should be exactly those, so a drift in either is caught.
Any crash found becomes a committed regression seed, per `docs/fuzzing.md`.

title: test: property tests for the delegate tree invariants
description: Generate random delegate trees and assert the invariants `WithDelegates` and `ValidateDelegateOrder` promise, at every depth.
why: The ordering rule is the one place a wrong answer is rejected by the host before the account contract runs, and the current tests use a handful of hand-built trees. The interesting cases — deep nesting, the same address at several levels, mixed address types, adjacent addresses that differ in one byte — are not among them.
criteria: Generated trees are always sorted at every level after `WithDelegates`, and always pass `ValidateDelegateOrder`.
A duplicate within a level is always rejected; the same address at different levels is always accepted.
Sorting is idempotent, and the result is independent of input order — asserted over generated permutations.
Deterministic seeded subset in CI, per the repo's existing property-test convention.
guidance: `gopter` is already a dependency and the repo has a documented property-test convention — follow it.
Generate adjacent-by-one-byte addresses deliberately; a comparison bug hides there and nowhere else.
Cap generated depth below `MaxDecodeDepth` so a refusal is not mistaken for a failure.

title: test(e2e): expired signature is rejected on-chain
description: A live scenario submitting an entry whose `signatureExpirationLedger` has passed, asserting the specific host error.
why: The expiration bound's inclusivity is documented from the host source and asserted in unit tests, and never checked against a real network. It is also the rule most likely to be off by one, because the JS SDK documents it the other way round.
criteria: Submits at a ledger past the expiration and asserts the specific rejection, not merely that the transaction failed.
A companion submission at exactly the expiration ledger succeeds, which is what proves the bound is inclusive.
The raw host error is logged verbatim in `e2e/RESULTS.md`.
The scenario skips cleanly rather than failing if the ledger cannot be hit precisely, and says so.
guidance: `CONTRIBUTING.md` is explicit that a rejection test asserting only 'it failed' passes for the wrong reason — assert which failure.
Hitting an exact ledger is timing-sensitive; poll `getLatestLedger` rather than assuming a rate.
The boundary pass is the harder and more valuable half; do not ship only the failure case.

title: test(e2e): nonce replay is rejected on-chain
description: Submit a valid entry, then submit a second transaction reusing the same address and nonce, asserting the host's rejection.
why: The nonce exists so an entry cannot be replayed, and that claim is currently sourced from reading the host rather than from observing it. It is also the claim the new batch-collision check is built on, so it ought to be grounded.
criteria: The first submission succeeds and is confirmed in a ledger; the second is rejected with the specific nonce error, logged verbatim.
A control submission with a fresh nonce succeeds afterwards, proving the account is not simply broken.
Both transaction hashes recorded in `e2e/RESULTS.md` with explorer links.
The scenario is independent of other scenarios' accounts, so it cannot be poisoned by them.
guidance: The enforcing pass will catch this locally, so the scenario has to skip it deliberately — `e2e/README.md` documents how the existing rejection scenarios do that.
Use a freshly funded account so the nonce state is known.
Report the raw error; a paraphrase is not evidence.

title: test(e2e): multisig threshold not met is rejected on-chain
description: A scenario where an account requiring two signers is given one, asserting the host rejects it.
why: Scenario C proves `AccountMultiSigner` is accepted when the threshold is met. The complementary case — that one signature on a two-of-two account is actually refused — is what proves the threshold is doing anything, and it is untested.
criteria: The same account and thresholds as the passing scenario, differing only in the signatures supplied.
Asserts the specific host error rather than a generic failure.
The raw error is recorded in `e2e/RESULTS.md`.
Shares the account setup with the passing scenario so the two cannot drift apart.
guidance: `refactor(e2e): reduce duplication across scenario runners` from Wave 9 built the shared harness — use it.
Assert which failure, not that something failed; an instruction-budget exhaustion would otherwise pass as a success.
The contrast with the passing scenario is the evidence, so run both in the same session.

title: test(e2e): three-level nested delegate tree on testnet
description: A live scenario with delegates nested three levels deep, every node signed, submitted and confirmed.
why: CAP-71-01 allows arbitrary nesting and the deepest tree ever submitted from this repo is one level. Whether the host walks a deeper tree the way the library assumes is an assumption, not a result.
criteria: A real three-level tree deployed and submitted, with the hash and ledger recorded.
The submitted envelope is decoded back and the observed tree shape logged, rather than assumed from what was built.
The per-node signatures are confirmed to be over the same payload, which is the CAP's central claim.
`e2e/RESULTS.md` records the run with explorer links.
guidance: `e2e/contracts/modular-account` delegates to addresses it stores; chaining instances gives the depth.
Two simulation passes are required, per CAP-71-01 — the record-sign-enforce flow is not optional here.
If the host behaves differently from the library's assumption, stop and report it; that is the most valuable possible outcome.

title: test: cross-version compatibility of entries and vectors
description: Assert that entries and vectors produced by an earlier release of this library still verify and still diff correctly against the current code.
why: Entries are pre-signed and stored. If a future change alters how one is read, an entry signed last month stops verifying, and nothing in CI would notice — the vectors are regenerated alongside the code, so they move together.
criteria: A frozen set of entries from the `v0.1.0` tag, committed separately from the regenerated vectors.
A test asserting each still verifies and inspects as it did, with the expected results committed.
The frozen set is explicitly never regenerated, and a check prevents it being rewritten by `make vectors`.
A documented process for adding a frozen set at each release.
guidance: The whole value is that this set does not move with the code — keep it well away from `testdata/vectors`.
`test: version the golden vector schema` from Wave 9 is related; read it so the two schemes agree.
If a frozen entry ever stops verifying, that is a wire-format regression and must stop the build.

title: test: per-package coverage floors with a documented rationale
description: Replace the single repository coverage floor with per-package floors, set from current measured values and justified per package.
why: One global floor lets a well-covered package subsidise a thin one. The packages where coverage matters most — the root signing path — are averaged together with the CLI and the examples, so a real regression in the former can hide behind the latter.
criteria: A committed per-package floor table with the measured current value and a one-line reason for each.
CI fails naming the package and both numbers when one drops.
The signing-path packages carry a strictly higher floor than the rest, stated as policy.
A deliberate drop proves the gate bites, shown in the PR and not committed.
guidance: Set floors from measurement, not aspiration; a floor nobody can meet gets raised away.
Coverage is not correctness — say so in the policy, and point at the mutation-testing work as the stronger check.
Packages with no tests by design (examples) should be excluded explicitly, not given a floor of zero.

title: test: soak test for the batch signing path
description: A long-running test signing large batches continuously, watching for leaked goroutines, unbounded memory and pool corruption.
why: `internal/xdrcopy` shares encoder and decoder buffers through `sync.Pool`, and `batch_sign.go` runs concurrently. The race detector covers correctness under contention for the duration of a test; it says nothing about what happens over hours, which is how the service actually runs.
criteria: Runs under a build tag or long flag so it never slows the normal suite.
Asserts goroutine count and heap in use return to a baseline after each round, with the tolerance justified.
Output bytes are checked against the golden vectors throughout, so corruption is caught and not merely leakage.
Scheduled in CI alongside the existing long-running jobs, with a committed report from a real run.
guidance: A pooled buffer handed to two callers is the failure this is looking for — asserting bytes, not just memory, is what would catch it.
`TestCopyConcurrentReuse` exists for the short version; this is the long one, not a replacement.
Report the real numbers from a real run; a soak test nobody has run is not evidence.

title: test: adversarial corpus of malformed entries
description: A committed corpus of deliberately hostile entries — depth bombs, huge argument lists, non-canonical strkeys, truncated XDR, inconsistent unions — with the expected refusal for each.
why: Every public entry point decodes input from elsewhere. The decode bound and the strkey check were each added in response to a specific concern; there is no single place that asserts the whole family is handled, so the next entry point added inherits none of that hardening by default.
criteria: Each case names the expected sentinel error, so the test asserts which refusal and not merely that one happened.
Every public entry point that takes an entry — `Inspect`, `Verify`, `DiffEntries`, `AuthorizeEntry`, `Decode*`, the CLI, the service — is run against the whole corpus.
A test that fails when a new public entry point is not covered, rather than a comment asking people to remember.
No case causes a panic, a hang, or unbounded allocation.
guidance: Reuse the frozen divergence corpus in `testdata/differential/regressions` for cases already known; do not duplicate them.
The coverage check over entry points is what keeps this from going stale — model it on `errors_meta_test.go`.
A case that currently is not refused is a finding: report it before fixing it.

title: test: assert the wasm core and the Go library agree exhaustively
description: Extend the wasm parity check from replaying the golden vectors to replaying the fuzz and differential corpora.
why: `make wasm-check` replays the vectors through the wasm core, which proves agreement on the cases someone thought of. The wasm build is a second compilation of the same code under a different toolchain and a different integer and memory model, so the cases that would diverge are the generated ones.
criteria: The differential and fuzz corpora replayed through the wasm core with byte equality asserted.
Any divergence is frozen as a regression case, per the existing convention.
Runs in the wasm CI job within a stated time budget.
A report of how many cases are covered, before and after.
guidance: `wasm/parity.mjs` is the existing harness; extend it rather than writing a second one.
`js/wasm` differs from native in number handling — the int64 nonce boundaries are the first place to look.
`docs/parity.md` frames what agreement proves; keep that framing.

title: test: benchmark regression gate per credential arm
description: Extend the signing-path budget check from one aggregate number to a per-arm, per-operation budget with its own threshold.
why: `scripts/checkbench` gates the signing path against a budget. One number means a regression in the delegates arm can be masked by an improvement in the legacy arm, and the delegates arm is the one that scales with tree size.
criteria: Separate budgets per arm for signing, verification and diffing, with committed baselines and justified thresholds.
Failure names the arm, the operation, the baseline and the measured value.
A delegate-tree benchmark parameterised by node count, so super-linear growth is visible.
A deliberate regression proves the gate bites, shown in the PR and not committed.
guidance: `scripts/checkbench` and the existing budget job are the starting point; do not add a parallel mechanism.
Set thresholds from repeated runs on the CI runner, not from one local measurement — noise is the reason these gates get disabled.
No floats in library code; this is tooling, so the constraint does not bind, but keep the comparison integer-based where you can.

title: test: golden vectors at every structural boundary
description: Vectors at the structural limits: maximum delegate nesting, maximum signatures on a multisig account, an empty argument list, a single-node tree, and the widest tree the generator can build.
why: Wave 9 added expiration boundary vectors. The structural boundaries got no equivalent treatment, and the host enforces limits there too — `MAX_ACCOUNT_SIGNATURES` is 20, and the library's own `MaxDecodeDepth` is 64.
criteria: A vector at exactly 20 account signatures, and a unit test proving 21 is refused with `ErrTooManySignatures`.
A vector at the deepest nesting the pinned JS SDK will produce, with the depth recorded in the vector's name.
Vectors for an empty argument list and a single-delegate tree.
All generated, none hand-edited, and `make vectors-check` green.
guidance: Cite the host constant for the signature cap rather than trusting the number in this description.
If the JS SDK refuses a depth the Go library accepts, that disagreement is the finding — report it, do not paper over it.
Keep vector names descriptive of the boundary, since that is how the next person finds them.

title: test: reproducible e2e runs against a local Stellar quickstart
description: Let the e2e suite run against a local quickstart container as well as testnet, so the scenarios are reproducible offline and in CI without friendbot.
why: Every e2e scenario needs testnet and friendbot, which makes them slow, rate-limited, and unavailable when testnet is unhealthy. A contributor who cannot run them does not run them, and reviews the delegate scenarios by reading.
criteria: The suite selects network by configuration, with the same scenarios passing against both.
Account funding works without friendbot in the local case.
`make e2e-local` or equivalent documented, from a clean checkout.
A run against both recorded, with the protocol version each reported.
guidance: `SOROAUTH_RPC_URL` already exists and the suite verifies the endpoint with a live call — extend that rather than branching on a flag everywhere.
A local network may run a different protocol version; report it rather than assuming parity with testnet.
Testnet remains the evidence of record for `RESULTS.md`; local is for iteration. Say which is which.

title: feat(cmd): soroauth simulate
description: A subcommand that runs the record pass against an RPC endpoint and prints the returned entries, resources and minimum fee.
why: The CLI can sign, inspect, verify and diff an entry but cannot obtain one. Getting an unsigned entry means writing a Go program or hand-driving curl, which puts the CLI's whole workflow out of reach of someone exploring.
criteria: Takes a transaction envelope, runs the record pass, prints each entry as base64 with its operation and entry index.
Reports the arm the host actually recorded, decoded from the response rather than assumed.
`--json` output composes with the other subcommands, as the existing `--json` contract requires.
A simulation error is reported with the host's message and a non-zero exit code.
guidance: The parsing belongs in `rpcflow`; this subcommand should be a thin front end to it.
Tests must not touch the network — drive them from committed response fixtures.
`--rpc-url` and `$SOROAUTH_RPC_URL` already exist on other subcommands; follow that convention exactly.

title: feat(cmd): soroauth submit
description: A subcommand that runs the enforcing pass with signed entries, assembles, submits and polls to completion.
why: With `simulate` and `sign` present, submission is the missing step that turns the CLI from a decoder into something that completes the flow — and the two-pass requirement is exactly what people get wrong by hand.
criteria: Runs the enforcing pass with the signed entries, so the submitted fee covers the signatures.
Prints the transaction hash before polling, so a timeout still leaves the user something to look up.
Polls to a terminal state and exits non-zero on failure, reporting the host's error verbatim.
Refuses to submit if an address entry is unsigned, unless explicitly overridden.
guidance: `rpcflow.SignAndSubmit` already implements this flow — reuse it rather than writing a second one.
The envelope signing key must come from an environment variable, never a flag, like `sign`.
Printing the hash before polling matters: that is the difference between a recoverable and an unrecoverable timeout.

title: feat(cmd): batch mode reading many entries from a file
description: Let the entry-taking subcommands read a newline-delimited or JSON list of entries and emit one result per input.
