why: Every subcommand takes exactly one entry, so processing a batch means a shell loop that starts a process per entry and, worse, usually drops the error from one iteration.
criteria: Supported by `inspect`, `verify`, `diff` and `sign`, with one consistent input and output format.
A per-entry failure is reported with its index and does not silently end the run; the exit code reflects that something failed.
`--json` emits one array or one object per line, documented, so it composes with `jq`.
The all-or-nothing rule is honoured for `sign`: a batch that cannot be fully signed produces no signed output.
guidance: `AuthorizeAll` already defines the all-or-nothing semantics for signing — the CLI must not loosen them.
Choose one streaming format and document it; two half-supported formats is worse than one.
Never echo an entry into an error message, per the CLI's existing rule.

title: feat(cmd): configuration file for the CLI
description: Let the CLI read defaults — network, RPC URL, secret variable name, output format — from a config file, with a documented precedence order.
why: Every invocation repeats `--network` and `--rpc-url`. Repetition invites shell aliases and history, and history is where a mistyped network silently becomes the default.
criteria: Documented precedence: flag, then environment, then file, then built-in default.
`soroauth doctor` reports which file was loaded and which value came from where.
No secret value may be stored in the file; only the name of an environment variable, with a test asserting a secret-shaped value is refused.
A missing file is not an error; an unparseable one is.
guidance: Standard library only, per the CLI's constraint — choose a format the standard library can parse.
Refusing to hold secrets is the security-relevant decision; make it explicit and tested rather than documented.
`doctor` reporting the resolved source is what makes a precedence bug findable.

title: feat(cmd): exec-based external signer
description: Let `soroauth sign` delegate to an external program over a documented protocol on stdin and stdout, so any signer can be used without a Go dependency.
why: The CLI can sign with a seed from the environment and nothing else. Every KMS, HSM and hardware signer in the repo is unreachable from the command line, which is where someone would most want to try one.
criteria: A documented protocol passing the preimage and payload and receiving the signature `ScVal`.
The signature is validated as well-formed before being written into the entry; a malformed response is an error naming what was wrong.
The helper's non-zero exit, timeout and malformed output are three distinct errors.
No secret is passed to the helper on the command line or in the environment by this mechanism.
guidance: `remote/protocol.go` already defines a signing protocol over HTTP — reuse its message shapes so there is one contract in two transports.
Passing the preimage, not just the payload, is what lets the helper show a user what they are approving.
Validate the returned `ScVal` — the CLI must not write arbitrary bytes into an entry because a helper said so.

title: ci: SLSA build provenance and signed release artifacts
description: Generate build provenance for every released artifact, sign them, and document how a consumer verifies both.
why: The release workflow publishes binaries and a container image. Nothing about them is verifiable, so a consumer cannot distinguish a real release from a convincing one — which for a library that produces signatures is the supply-chain risk that matters.
criteria: Provenance attestations generated in the release workflow for every artifact.
Artifacts signed, with verification commands documented in the README and actually run in CI.
An SBOM published per release.
A deliberately tampered artifact fails verification, demonstrated in the PR.
guidance: Keyless signing keeps a long-lived key out of CI; if you choose a key, justify it.
The demonstration that verification rejects a tampered artifact is the evidence — without it this is configuration nobody has tested.
Coordinate with the multi-arch image issue so the image and the binaries are covered by one scheme.

title: ci: reproducible builds with a verification job
description: Make the released binaries byte-reproducible from a tagged source tree, and add a job that rebuilds and compares.
why: Provenance says who built an artifact. Reproducibility lets anyone check what was built. For a signing library the two together are what make a release auditable by someone who does not trust the CI.
criteria: Documented build command producing byte-identical binaries for each target from a clean checkout.
A CI job rebuilding the latest release and comparing checksums, failing on any difference.
Every source of non-determinism — paths, timestamps, build IDs — identified and neutralised, and the list documented.
Instructions a third party can follow to reproduce, verified by someone other than the author.
guidance: `-trimpath` and a pinned toolchain are the start; module cache state and VCS stamping are the usual remaining culprits.
The CLI embeds version, commit and Go version — make sure that stamping is deterministic given the same inputs.
If a target cannot be made reproducible, say which and why rather than quietly excluding it.

title: ci: CodeQL and dependency review on pull requests
description: Add static security analysis and dependency review, with findings triaged rather than merely collected.
why: `cspell` mentions a `codeql` word and nothing runs it. A library that decodes untrusted input and handles key material has exactly the shape static analysis is good at, and dependency review is the cheapest guard against a malicious transitive update.
criteria: CodeQL runs on pull requests and on a schedule, with the Go query suite.
Dependency review blocks a pull request introducing a known-vulnerable dependency.
Existing findings are triaged: fixed, or dismissed with a written reason.
Pull-request check count stays within the repository's stated cap, or the cap is revisited deliberately.
guidance: `CONTRIBUTING.md` says pull requests are capped at three checks and explains why — respect that or change it explicitly.
A scanner whose findings nobody reads is worse than none; the triage is the deliverable.
Pin the actions by commit SHA, as every other workflow here does.

title: ci: nightly build against the Go SDK's main branch
description: A scheduled job building and testing against `go-stellar-sdk@main`, reporting breakage without failing the pinned build.
why: `docs/sdk-support.md` sets a policy for moving the pin, and the pin moves when someone tries it. Finding out at that moment that the SDK changed an XDR type is the expensive version; finding out the night it lands is cheap.
criteria: Runs on a schedule against the SDK's default branch, isolated so it cannot affect the pinned build's status.
On breakage it opens or updates a single tracking issue rather than emitting a notification per run.
The golden vectors are part of what it runs, since a wire-format change there is the finding that matters most.
A green run is visible somewhere, so silence is distinguishable from a broken job.
guidance: A scheduled job that only speaks up on failure is indistinguishable from one that has stopped running — make success observable.
One rolling issue, not one per night; a noisy bot gets muted and then ignored.
`ci-parity.yml` already runs on a schedule — follow its conventions for staggering.

title: ci: enforce that every public entry point bounds its input
description: A check that every exported function taking an entry, envelope or base64 blob goes through the bounded decoder rather than the SDK's default.
why: `decode.go` exists because the SDK's default limits are much looser than this library wants. The bound only helps where it is used, and nothing stops the next exported function from calling `xdr.SafeUnmarshalBase64` directly — which is how the hardening quietly stops covering the newest code.
criteria: A check over the AST that fails naming any exported function reaching the SDK decoder directly.
Deliberate exceptions are explicit and annotated, not implicit.
It fails on a newly added violation, demonstrated in the PR and not committed.
It fails loudly if it finds no entry points at all, so it cannot pass vacuously.
guidance: `errors_meta_test.go` and `internal/doccheck` are the models: turn a prose rule into a check that bites.
A test is enough; it need not be a separate CI job, given the check-count cap.
The vacuous-pass guard matters — a scanner that silently matches nothing is the failure mode here.

title: ci: publish the documentation as a browsable site
description: Build the eighteen documents in `docs/` into a navigable site published on each release, with search and the Go API reference linked.
why: `docs/README.md` is a hand-maintained map of eighteen documents, which works for someone already in the repository and not for someone deciding whether to use the library. Nothing is cross-linked or searchable.
criteria: Every document reachable, with working internal links, checked by the existing link checker.
Published automatically on release; no manual step.
A version selector or a clear statement of which version the site documents.
`docs/README.md` remains correct, or becomes generated from the same source rather than duplicating it.
guidance: The repository is the source of truth; the site renders it. Do not let content move into a generator's templates.
`links.yml` already checks links — keep it covering the sources so the site cannot ship broken ones.
Avoid a second place to update when adding a document; generate the navigation.

title: feat(cmd): shell-completable dynamic values
description: Extend completions beyond subcommands and flag names to flag values — networks, output formats, and addresses present in a supplied entry.
why: Completions cover names, so a mistyped `--network pubic` is still a silent fall-through to a literal passphrase. Completing values is where completion actually prevents an error rather than saving keystrokes.
criteria: The three named networks and every enumerable format complete in bash, zsh and fish.
Addresses complete from an entry already named on the command line, where the shell allows it.
The existing spec table stays the single source, so the completion test keeps catching drift.
No completion path can execute an entry's contents or run a signer.
guidance: `commandSpecs` in `completions.go` is the source of truth and a test already asserts it matches the usage text — extend it, do not fork it.
Dynamic completion that shells out is a code-execution surface; keep it to parsing, and say so.
A literal passphrase must remain possible — completion suggests, it must not constrain.

title: feat(cmd): machine-readable error output for every subcommand
description: Give `--json` errors a stable schema — a code, a message, and the offending field — rather than a single free-text `error` string.
why: `writeJSONError` emits `{"error": "..."}`. A caller that needs to branch has to match on prose, which is not a contract and changes whenever a message is improved. The library already has sentinel errors; the CLI flattens them away.
criteria: A documented schema with a stable code per sentinel error, versioned so a change is detectable.
Every subcommand emits it, asserted by a test over all of them rather than per subcommand.
No error payload contains an entry, a secret or a key, with a test asserting it.
The exit code and the code in the payload always agree, asserted.
guidance: `errors.go`'s sentinels are the natural code set; map them explicitly rather than deriving codes from message text.
A test that iterates every subcommand is what stops the next one from being added without this.
Keep the human output unchanged; this is the machine contract.

title: chore: split the root package along its seams
description: Assess whether the thirty-one files and roughly 490 exported symbols in the root package should be split into subpackages, and either do it behind an unchanged public surface or record why not.
why: The root package has grown from the eleven files the design called for to thirty-one, spanning signing, verification, inspection, risk analysis, planning, coordination, TUI and WebAuthn. Whether that is one coherent package or several is now a real question, and answering it after the API has more consumers is harder.
criteria: A written assessment of the seams, with the dependency graph between current files as evidence.
If split: the public import path and every exported name are unchanged, proven by a compile-time check against the current surface.
Every golden vector and parity suite stays green, proving the move is behaviour-preserving.
If not split: the reasoning is committed, so the question is settled rather than re-raised.
guidance: Deciding not to split is a legitimate and valuable outcome — the deliverable is the decision with its evidence.
A `go/ast` snapshot of the exported surface, compared before and after, is what makes 'unchanged' a fact rather than a claim.
Do not combine this with any behaviour change; a refactor whose diff includes a fix cannot be verified by the vectors.

title: chore: generate the CLI reference from the command specs
description: Generate the README's CLI section, the man page and the completions from one source, so none can drift from the flags the code actually parses.
why: The man page and completions already derive from `commandSpecs`, and the README's CLI section is written by hand — nine subcommands documented in prose beside a spec table that a test checks against real flag parsing. The README is the copy that drifts.
criteria: The README's CLI flag documentation is generated or checked against the specs, failing CI on divergence.
A new subcommand or flag cannot be added without the documentation following, demonstrated by adding one in the PR and showing the check fire.
Hand-written prose and examples survive — only the flag tables are generated.
The generated output is committed, so the README is readable on GitHub without a build step.
guidance: `TestSpecsCoverTheUsageText` already proves this approach works for completions; extend the same idea to the README.
Do not generate the explanatory prose: the CLI section's value is the explanation, and a generator would flatten it.
Keep the committed output in the diff so a reviewer sees what changed.

title: chore: a release checklist that CI enforces
description: Turn the release process into a preflight job that verifies the conditions before a tag is published rather than a document someone follows.
why: Releasing currently depends on remembering: CHANGELOG updated, vectors regenerated, version bumped, docs consistent, every workflow green. Each of those is checkable, and the one that gets forgotten is the one that matters.
criteria: A job asserting: CHANGELOG has an entry for the version, the vectors are reproducible, every workflow is green on the commit, and no document references a stale version.
It blocks the release workflow rather than reporting afterwards.
It checks every workflow's conclusion on the exact commit, not just the required checks — the gap that let a red `spellcheck` reach main.
A deliberately incomplete release is refused, demonstrated in the PR.
guidance: Checking all workflows on the commit, not the pull request's checks, is the specific lesson from the `spellcheck` incident — see the 'Editing a workflow' section in CONTRIBUTING.
Reuse the release workflow; this is a gate in front of it, not a replacement.
A checklist in a document is what is being replaced — resist adding another one.

title: feat(api): errors.Join for batch failures
description: Where a batch operation can fail for several independent reasons, report all of them with `errors.Join` instead of only the first.
why: `AuthorizeAll` returns on the first failure, so a caller with three unsigned entries fixes one, reruns, and finds the next. Each round trip through a batch of entries is cheap for the library and slow for the person.
criteria: Validation failures that can be collected are collected; the first signing failure still stops immediately, since signing has side effects.
`errors.Is` continues to match every joined sentinel, asserted by test.
The all-or-nothing contract is unchanged: still no partial results.
Each joined error still names its entry index and address.
guidance: Separate validation from execution: collecting pre-flight problems is safe, continuing past a signer failure is not.
`errors.Join` preserves `errors.Is` across all wrapped errors — add a test proving it for a joined pair.
Do not change any existing error's text beyond what joining requires.

title: feat(api): Equal and Clone helpers for entries
description: Exported `Equal` and `Clone` for `SorobanAuthorizationEntry`, with semantics stated: byte equality and an unaliased deep copy.
why: `internal/xdrcopy` is internal, so callers write their own deep copy — usually a struct assignment, which aliases the pointers and slices the XDR types are full of. That is the exact bug the repo's own no-mutation rule exists to prevent, and external callers get no help with it.
criteria: `Clone` returns a copy sharing no memory with its input, asserted by a test that mutates the copy and checks the original.
`Equal` is XDR byte equality, documented as such, and distinguished in the doc comment from semantic equivalence.
An encoding failure is an error, never a false from `Equal` or a zero value from `Clone`.
A fuzz target asserting `Equal(e, Clone(e))` holds for arbitrary entries.
guidance: Thin exported wrappers over `internal/xdrcopy`, not a second implementation.
Say plainly that `Equal` is byte equality: two entries that differ only in delegate order are unequal here and both may be valid.
`xdrcopy` pools buffers; make sure the exported path is safe for concurrent use and test it under `-race`.

title: feat(api): iterator over credential nodes
description: An exported iterator over an entry's credential nodes, yielding address, path and signature state for each.
why: `Inspect` returns a nested `EntryInfo` that a caller must walk recursively to answer 'which nodes are unsigned' — which the docs tell every caller to check before submitting. `credentialNodes` does exactly this internally and is unexported.
criteria: Yields the top-level node and every delegate at every depth, in a documented stable order.
Carries the path string `DiffEntries` uses, so findings from the two can be correlated.
Read-only: the iterator cannot be used to write a signature.
Depth-bounded like every other traversal, with a test proving a pathological tree is refused.
guidance: Use the `iter.Seq` form the Go version in `go.mod` supports, and say so in the doc comment.
Reuse `diff.go`'s path scheme rather than inventing a second one; correlating the two is the point.
Read-only matters: the internal walker returns pointers for writing, and that must not leak.

title: feat(api): sentinel error for an unsupported invocation function type
description: Add a sentinel for an invocation whose function type the library does not handle, and use it instead of falling through to generic handling.
why: An unrecognised `SorobanAuthorizedFunctionType` is currently handled generically — byte-compared in `diff.go`, reported with a numeric fallback name in the tree renderer. The repo's tie-break rule is to fail closed, and a silently generic answer about what an entry authorizes is the opposite.
criteria: A new exported sentinel, with a test that produces it, as the sentinel meta-test requires.
Every reader of the invocation tree either handles the type or returns the sentinel; none reports a generic description.
A test constructing an out-of-range function type asserts the sentinel from each reader.
`errors.go`'s documentation explains when a caller should expect it.
guidance: Decide deliberately whether `Inspect` should fail or report — and say which reading you chose in the commit, per the tie-break rule.
Do not break the two real arms: `contract_fn` and the create arms must behave exactly as they do today.
The vectors prove the real arms are unaffected; run them.

title: feat(api): expose the decode limits as documented constants
description: Audit the decode limits in `decode.go`, make each an exported documented constant, and let a caller tighten them.
why: `MaxDecodeDepth` is exported at 64; other limits in the same file may not be, and the number is a policy choice a caller with stricter requirements cannot express. A caller who wants depth 8 has to validate separately and hope the two checks agree.
criteria: Every limit is an exported constant with a doc comment saying what it protects against and why that value.
An options form lets a caller supply stricter limits; looser than the default is refused.
Refusals cite the limit that was hit, which the existing `ErrDecodeLimit` message already does for depth.
A test per limit proving it is enforced at the boundary, not one past it.
guidance: Tightening only: allowing a caller to loosen the bound would turn a safety default into a footgun.
`decode.go` has the rationale for bounding at all; extend it rather than restating it.
Keep the default behaviour byte-identical — the vectors are the check.

title: feat(api): String methods for the exported report types
description: Give `EntryInfo`, `VerificationReport` and the risk findings `String` methods, as `EntryDiff` has.
why: `EntryDiff.String()` renders a readable report and the CLI uses it. `EntryInfo` and `VerificationReport` have no equivalent, so the CLI formats them itself and any other consumer formats them again, differently.
criteria: Each renders the same information the CLI currently prints, verdict or summary first.
The CLI is refactored onto them, so there is one renderer per type and no drift.
A golden-output test per type, so a formatting change is a visible diff rather than a surprise.
No `String` method panics or allocates unboundedly on a pathological value.
guidance: `EntryDiff.String()` is the model: lead with the line that answers the reader's actual question.
Do not let `String` imply a verdict the type cannot support — a `cannot_check` must read as such.
Golden-output tests make these safe to change later; without them nobody will touch the formatting.

title: test: assert every exported function checks its context
description: A meta-test asserting that every exported function taking a `context.Context` checks `ctx.Err()` before doing work and has a cancellation test.
why: `CONTRIBUTING.md` states this rule and Wave 9 audited it once by hand. An audit is a snapshot; the rule only holds if something checks it when the next context-taking function is added.
criteria: Parses the package for exported functions whose first parameter is a `context.Context`, and fails naming any without a cancellation test.
Fails loudly if it finds no such functions, so it cannot pass vacuously.
Every current function passes, and any that did not before being fixed is named in the PR.
Covers the adapter modules too, or states why it cannot reach them.
guidance: `errors_meta_test.go` is the pattern: parse the source, scan the tests, fail with names.
Be loose about how the test asserts cancellation and strict about its existence, exactly as the sentinel check is.
The vacuous-pass guard is not optional; it is the failure mode of every check like this.

title: test: golden vectors for a muxed address in an invocation argument
description: Vectors where an invocation argument contains a muxed (`M…`) address, which `ParseAddress` rejects for credentials but which is legal inside arguments.
why: `ParseAddress` rejects `M…` because credentials must name the account itself. An argument is a different position with a different rule, and nothing tests that the library passes such an argument through untouched rather than rejecting the whole entry.
criteria: A vector with a muxed address argument, generated by the pinned JS SDK, byte-equal through the Go path.
`Inspect` and `DiffEntries` handle it without error.
A test asserting `ParseAddress` still rejects `M…` for credentials, so the two rules stay distinct.
`docs/glossary.md` or the `ParseAddress` doc comment states the distinction.
guidance: Confirm from the XDR that a muxed address is representable in an `ScVal` argument before building the vector; if it is not, report that and close the issue with the finding.
The two positions having different rules is the thing worth documenting, whichever way the vector comes out.
Never hand-edit a vector.

title: test: parity harnesses cover the delegates arm explicitly
description: Audit the Python and Rust parity harnesses for delegate-arm coverage and add the cases they are missing.
why: `docs/parity.md` states what agreement proves. If the harnesses only recompute the legacy and V2 vectors, that agreement says nothing about the delegates arm — which is the newest wire format and the one most likely to diverge.
criteria: A written statement of which vectors each harness currently covers, from reading the harness rather than assuming.
Every delegates-arm vector covered by both, or a recorded reason a given SDK cannot express one.
The parity report artifact states coverage per arm.
`docs/parity.md` updated to say what is and is not covered.
guidance: Start by measuring; the audit may show coverage is already complete, which is a perfectly good result to report.
A harness that silently skips a vector is the failure mode — make skips explicit and counted.
If an SDK genuinely cannot build a delegates entry, that is a finding about that SDK, not a gap to paper over.

title: test: assert e2e scenarios are independent and reorderable
description: Run the e2e scenarios in a shuffled order and in isolation, to prove none depends on another's accounts or ledger state.
why: The scenarios share a fixture harness and all run against one network. A scenario that passes only because an earlier one funded an account is a scenario that will fail alone, and nothing currently distinguishes the two.
criteria: Each scenario passes when run alone by name.
The suite passes with scenarios shuffled, with the seed reported so a failure is reproducible.
Any discovered dependency is fixed or documented as deliberate with its reason.
`e2e/README.md` states the independence property so it is a rule rather than an accident.
guidance: `refactor(e2e): reduce duplication across scenario runners` built the shared harness — shared setup is fine, shared mutable state is not.
Report the shuffle seed on failure; a flaky ordering bug is unfixable without it.
Friendbot rate limits may make isolated runs slow; that is a reason to document the cost, not to skip the check.

title: test: fuzz the canonical JSON round trip
description: A fuzz target asserting XDR → canonical JSON → XDR is the identity for arbitrary decoded entries.
why: A canonical JSON encoding is only useful if it is exact. A field that silently fails to round-trip turns the encoding from a representation into a lossy summary, and table tests will not find which field.
criteria: Asserts byte-identical XDR after a round trip, for every entry the bounded decoder accepts.
Input the encoding cannot represent exactly must be refused by the encoder, not silently altered — asserted.
Seed corpus from the golden vectors.
Wired into the continuous fuzzing workflow.
guidance: Depends on the canonical JSON issue; check its state first and say so on the issue.
The refusal assertion is as important as the identity one: a lossy success is the dangerous outcome.
Any crash becomes a committed regression seed, per `docs/fuzzing.md`.

title: test: assert the container image runs the documented commands
description: A CI test that pulls the published image and runs each documented example command inside it.
why: The README documents the container image with example invocations. The image is built in CI and never exercised, so an image that builds but cannot run the CLI — a missing certificate bundle, a wrong entrypoint — would ship unnoticed.
criteria: Runs `--version`, `inspect`, `verify` and `diff` inside the image against committed fixtures.
Asserts the exit codes, not merely that the commands produced output.
Covers every architecture the image publishes.
Fails the release if the image cannot run the documented commands.
guidance: Test the published image, not a locally built one — the published artifact is what users get.
A command needing network must be excluded explicitly, with a note, rather than failing intermittently.
Coordinate with the multi-arch image issue so both architectures are covered once.

title: test: record and replay RPC fixtures for offline flow tests
description: A recorder that captures real RPC request and response pairs, and a replayer so `rpcflow` and the new RPC subcommands can be tested offline against real responses.
why: `rpcflow`'s tests use a hand-written fake client, which tests the code against the author's belief about the RPC's responses. The two-pass flow's correctness depends on details of real responses — which arm was recorded, what the fee came back as — and a fake cannot be wrong in the same ways the real thing is.
criteria: Recorded fixtures committed, each noting the RPC version, network and ledger it came from.
Replay is byte-faithful, and a fixture that does not match the request is an error rather than a silent miss.
`rpcflow`'s existing tests gain at least one real-fixture case alongside the fakes.
No fixture contains a secret, with a documented scrubbing step.
guidance: Keep the hand-written fakes for the failure injection they are good at; fixtures are for fidelity, not a replacement.
Record against testnet and say exactly when — an RPC response is a dated artifact.
A mismatched request must fail loudly: a replayer that falls through to a default is how an offline test passes against nothing.

title: feat(cmd): --quiet and --verbose output levels
description: Consistent verbosity control across subcommands: `--quiet` for exit-code-only use, `--verbose` for the reasoning behind a verdict.
why: Each subcommand prints one fixed amount. In a script the output is noise and the exit code is the signal; while debugging a refusal the output is too thin. Both users are currently served the same middle.
criteria: `--quiet` prints nothing on success and still exits with the right code, for every subcommand.
`--verbose` explains the verdict — which node, which rule, which field — without printing an entry or a secret.
Mutually exclusive, with a usage error if both are given.
Covered by a test iterating every subcommand, so a new one cannot omit them.
guidance: `--json` already exists and must be unaffected; verbosity governs the human output only.
Add the flags to `commandSpecs` so completions and the man page follow automatically.
`--verbose` must not become a channel for echoing input; the no-echo rule still holds.

title: feat(cmd): --network from an RPC endpoint's reported passphrase
description: Let `--network` be resolved by asking an RPC endpoint for its network passphrase, instead of being named or typed out.
why: A mistyped passphrase or the wrong named network produces a valid-looking signature over the wrong payload, which fails only on submission. The endpoint already knows the answer authoritatively, and asking it removes the class of error entirely.
criteria: A documented flag that fetches the passphrase from the configured RPC URL and uses it.
Reports the resolved passphrase before signing, so the user sees which network they are about to commit to.
A fetch failure is an error, never a fall-through to a default network.
Tests drive it from committed fixtures and touch no network.
guidance: Falling back to a default on failure would reintroduce exactly the bug this prevents — fail closed.
Printing the resolved value is the point; a silent correct answer teaches the user nothing.
The three named shorthands stay; this is an additional source, not a replacement.

title: ci: cache the Rust and Node toolchains across jobs
description: Audit cache usage across the workflows and add caching where a job rebuilds a toolchain or dependency tree it could reuse.
why: The contract build, the parity harnesses and the vector generator each install a toolchain. Slow CI is tolerated until it is not, and then the response is usually to run less of it — which is the outcome worth avoiding in a repo whose correctness gate is a regeneration.
criteria: Measured before-and-after wall-clock times per job, reported in the PR.
Cache keys include the lockfiles and toolchain pins, so a stale cache cannot mask a dependency change.
`make vectors-check` still regenerates from a clean state, since a cached generator output would defeat the gate.
No job's correctness depends on a cache hit, demonstrated by a cold run.
guidance: The drift check must not be cached in any way that lets it pass without regenerating; that is the one job where speed is not the priority.
Report real numbers — a caching change without measurement is a guess.
Pin the cache action by SHA like every other action here.

title: ci: fail the build on a stale generated artifact
description: One job that regenerates every generated artifact — vectors, corpora, man page, completions, diagrams — and fails if any committed copy differs.
why: `make vectors-check` does this for the vectors. The man page, completions, fuzz corpora and rendered diagrams are also generated and committed, and nothing checks them, so a committed copy can silently stop matching its source.
criteria: Every generated-and-committed artifact is covered, with a list in the job so a new one is an obvious omission.
Failure names the artifact and the command that regenerates it.
A deliberately stale artifact proves the gate bites, shown in the PR and not committed.
Runs within the repository's check-count cap, by extending an existing job rather than adding one.
guidance: `vectors-check` is the model and should be absorbed rather than duplicated.
Anything whose output is not deterministic cannot be checked this way — identify those and say so rather than making the job flaky.
Include the workflow file's own path in the `paths:` filter, or an edit to it will not run it.

title: chore: adopt a changelog-from-commits check
description: Check that every user-visible change since the last release has a CHANGELOG entry, using the conventional-commit prefixes already in use.
why: The commit format is conventional and enforced by convention, and the CHANGELOG is updated by hand. The entries that go missing are the ones added in a hurry, which correlates with the changes most worth announcing.
criteria: A check listing `feat` and `fix` commits since the last tag with no corresponding CHANGELOG line.
`chore`, `ci`, `test` and `docs` commits are excluded by default, with the policy documented.
Advisory on pull requests and blocking in the release preflight, so it does not become noise.
A missing entry is demonstrated to be caught, in the PR.
guidance: Do not generate the CHANGELOG from commits: the existing entries explain changes in a way commit subjects do not.
Matching commit to entry needs a rule — issue number or scope — so define it rather than guessing at text similarity.
Coordinate with the release-preflight issue so there is one gate.

title: feat(cmd): soroauth explain-error
description: A subcommand that takes a host or RPC error string and explains what it means for an authorization entry, with the source cited.
why: The failures this library's users hit come back as host error codes and terse strings. Mapping those to a cause — expiration passed, nonce consumed, resource budget exceeded because the enforcing pass was skipped — is knowledge currently spread across doc comments and the e2e README.
criteria: Covers the errors the e2e scenarios actually produced, each with the CAP or host source cited.
An unrecognised error is reported as unrecognised, never guessed at.
Suggests the concrete next check, such as re-running the enforcing pass.
Every mapping has a test, and the text is sourced from a real recorded error rather than invented.
guidance: `e2e/RESULTS.md` and the rejection scenarios are the corpus of real errors — use them as the input, not memory.
A wrong explanation is worse than none here: the user will act on it. Fail closed on anything not recognised.
Cite the host source for each explanation, as every protocol claim in this repo must.

title: chore: issue template for a wire-format or vector discrepancy
description: A dedicated issue template for reporting that two implementations disagree, or that a golden vector looks wrong.
why: The repo's rule is to stop and report rather than edit a vector to make a test pass. Nothing makes that easy: the bug template asks for reproduction steps, not for the two byte strings and which SDK produced each.
criteria: Collects both encodings, both implementation versions, the vector name, and the command that produced the disagreement.
States prominently that no vector may be edited by hand.
Routes to maintainers at the severity a wire-format disagreement deserves.
Linked from CONTRIBUTING's golden-vector section.
guidance: The security template already routes to private advisories — follow its structure for a template that must be read before filing.
Ask for the bytes. A prose description of a byte-level disagreement is not actionable.
Keep it short enough to be used; a long form is a form nobody fills in.

title: chore: measure and report CI cost per workflow
description: A scheduled report of runner minutes per workflow, so the cost of ten workflows is visible before it becomes a reason to delete one.
why: The repository now runs nine workflows plus continuous fuzzing, several on schedules. Nobody knows which ones dominate, so any future decision about what to cut would be made on impression rather than measurement.
criteria: A scheduled job reporting minutes per workflow over a trailing window.
Published where a maintainer will see it, not only in a log.
The report itself costs materially less than what it measures, and the PR says what it costs.
No credential beyond the token the job needs.
guidance: Use the Actions API rather than estimating from run counts and durations.
A scheduled job that only reports anomalies is invisible when healthy — make a normal week legible too.
Keep it advisory: this informs decisions, it should not gate anything.

title: chore: retire the Wave 9 issue script and archive its backlog
description: Remove `scripts/wave9_issues.py`, now superseded by `scripts/wave_issues.py`, and archive the Wave 9 backlog documents as a completed record with their outcomes.
why: Two scripts that create issues is one too many, and the older one hard-codes Wave 9's file names plus the twenty-one issues that predated it. Leaving both means the next person picks the wrong one. The Wave 9 documents are worth keeping as a record, but only if they say what actually happened.
criteria: `scripts/wave9_issues.py` removed, with anything it did that the new script does not reproduced first.
The Wave 9 backlog documents marked complete, recording which items shipped and which did not.
Every reference to the old script in the documentation updated.
A dry run of the new script against the Wave 9 backlog still produces a sensible plan, shown in the PR.
guidance: Check the old script for behaviour the new one lacks — it re-rendered existing issues from a Markdown backlog, which the new one does not do.
The archive should be honest about incomplete items; a record that lists only successes is not a record.
Do not weaken the new script's dry-run default or its duplicate-title guard while consolidating.

title: docs: threat model
description: A document stating what soroauth defends against, what it does not, and which component is responsible for each boundary.
why: `SECURITY.md` covers reporting and `docs/verification-limits.md` covers what verification proves. Nothing states the overall model, so a reader cannot tell whether a given risk — a compromised signer, a hostile entry, a malicious RPC — is in scope.
criteria: Enumerates the trust boundaries: caller, signer, RPC endpoint, entry source, network.
For each, what the library assumes, what it checks, and what it cannot check.
Cites the code that enforces each check, so a claim can be followed to its implementation.
States plainly that the library is unaudited, consistent with the README.
guidance: Every claim needs the file that implements it; a threat model nobody can verify is marketing.
A hostile RPC is a real and under-discussed case: it can lie about the entries to sign, and `--network` from an endpoint makes that sharper.
Be explicit about the limits rather than diplomatic; the honest version is the useful one.

title: docs: performance characteristics and when they matter
description: A document reporting measured costs of the main operations, how they scale, and which are dominated by the signer rather than the library.
why: Benchmarks and a budget check exist, and the numbers live only in CI. Someone sizing a service has nothing to read, and the most important fact — that a remote signer dominates everything the library does — is nowhere stated.
criteria: Measured numbers per operation and per arm, with the machine and Go version recorded.
Scaling with delegate count shown, since that is the one super-linear risk.
States plainly where the library's cost is irrelevant next to signer latency or RPC round trips.
Says how to reproduce every number.
guidance: Report what you measured, not what you expect; an unreproduced number is worse than none.
`scripts/checkbench` and the existing benchmarks are the source — do not invent a parallel harness.
Date the numbers. Performance documentation without a date is read as current forever.

title: docs: recipes for the ten most common tasks
description: A cookbook of short, complete, compiling examples for the tasks people actually arrive wanting.
why: The README has one quickstart and the guides are deep. Between them is the gap where most questions live: sign for a multisig account, sign one node of a delegate tree, check an entry before submitting, upgrade a simulated entry.
criteria: At least ten recipes, each a complete compiling program, not a fragment.
Covered by the README-snippet compilation check, so none can rot.
Each states the task in the reader's words and links the deeper guide.
No recipe prints or accepts a secret.
guidance: `internal/readmesnippets` already verifies snippets compile — extend it to cover these.
Complete programs: a fragment that does not compile is where documentation decays first.
Link rather than restate; the guides are the explanation and the recipe is the shortest path.

title: docs: the delegates arm end to end
description: One document following a delegates entry from construction through signing, verification and submission, with the protocol rule at each step.
why: The delegates arm is the newest and least familiar wire format, and its explanation is spread across `AuthorizeAll`'s doc comment, the multi-party guide, the glossary and the README. A newcomer has to assemble it from four places.
criteria: Follows one real entry through every step, with actual bytes or CLI output at each.
States at each step which CAP-71-01 rule applies and why.
Covers the three traps: ordering, the Void top-level signature, and the shared payload that makes the expiration fatal.
Links the existing documents rather than restating them.
guidance: Use a committed golden vector as the worked example so the bytes are real and reproducible.
The shared-payload consequence is the thing people get wrong — give it the most room.
Do not duplicate `docs/multi-party-signing.md`; this is the single-party structural walkthrough.

title: docs: what to do when a submission fails
description: A troubleshooting guide from the symptom a user sees to the cause and the check that confirms it.
why: The failure modes are known and documented in the places that cause them — the two-pass requirement in the README, the expiration rule in `expiration.go`, stale signatures in the diff docs. A user with a failed transaction does not know which of those to read.
criteria: Organised by symptom, since that is what the reader has.
Each entry names the confirming check: a CLI command or a library call.
Covers at minimum: resource budget exceeded, expiration passed, nonce consumed, wrong network, signature on the wrong node, unsigned delegate.
Every claim about host behaviour cites its source.
guidance: Start from the real errors in `e2e/RESULTS.md` and the rejection scenarios, not from imagined failures.
Give the command that confirms each cause; a guide that only names causes leaves the work undone.
Coordinate with the `explain-error` subcommand so the two agree.

title: docs: architecture decision records for the deliberate departures
description: Short ADRs for the decisions that differ from the obvious choice: the target-address rule, refusing to re-sign, no expiration cap, V2 by default, `cannot_check` as a verdict.
why: Each is explained in a doc comment at the point of use, which tells a reader what the code does and not why that was chosen over the alternative. The reasoning is in commit messages, which nobody reads at review time — so the decisions get re-argued.
criteria: One record per decision: context, the alternatives, the choice, and its consequences.
Each cites the code that implements it and the commit that introduced it.
Each records what would have to change for the decision to be revisited.
Indexed from `docs/README.md`.
guidance: The repo's commit bodies are unusually rich — mine them rather than reconstructing the reasoning.
Short records. An ADR nobody finishes reading does not preserve a decision.
Include at least one decision that is genuinely arguable, so the format is not just self-justification.

title: docs: how soroauth and soroauth-explain divide the problem
description: A document stating which library answers which question, and why interpreting an entry is deliberately not done here.
why: `soroauth-explain` now exists and the glossary points at it in one line. A user who wants to know what an entry authorizes needs to be told clearly that this library reports structure and that one reports meaning — otherwise they file the feature request here.
criteria: States the split: bytes and structure here, interpretation there.
Explains why they are separate — different honesty boundaries and different failure consequences.
Shows one entry through both, so the difference is concrete.
Linked from both repositories' READMEs.
guidance: Be accurate about `soroauth-explain`'s current state; check it rather than describing an intention.
`Inspect`'s doc comment already draws this line — be consistent with it.
Do not oversell either side; the value is the clarity of the boundary.

title: docs: operating the verification service
description: A runbook for running the service: configuration, deployment shape, what to monitor, what the alerts mean, and how to respond.
why: `docs/verification-service.md` says what the service does and what it refuses. Nothing says how to run it — what to watch, what a rising refusal rate means, or what to do when it stops responding.
criteria: Configuration reference with every option, its default and its effect.
The signals worth alerting on, with what each indicates.
Response steps for the likely failures, including a wedged signer and an unreachable RPC.
States the deployment assumptions, consistent with the threat model.
guidance: Coordinate with the metrics issue so the runbook names signals that exist.
Be honest about what the service does not do; a runbook implying high availability it has not been built for is a trap.
Base the failure list on what has actually gone wrong in testing, not a generic checklist.

title: docs: versioning and compatibility promises
description: State what stability the library promises for its Go API, its wire output, its CLI flags, its JSON shapes and its vector schema — each may differ.
why: Wave 9 produced a deprecation and support policy and a vector schema version. There is no single statement of what a consumer may rely on, and the answer genuinely differs per surface: wire output is fixed by the protocol, CLI output is not.
criteria: A promise per surface, with the version scheme that governs it.
States plainly which surfaces may change in a minor release.
Covers pre-1.0 expectations honestly rather than implying stability the version number does not claim.
Reconciled with `docs/sdk-support.md` and the deprecation policy, with no contradiction between them.
guidance: Check the existing policy documents first and extend rather than overlay; a contradictory second policy is worse than one.
The wire format is not this project's to change — say that explicitly, citing the CAPs.
Promise what will be kept. An aspirational promise is worse than a narrow one.

title: docs: contributing a new signer
description: A guide for adding a signer adapter: the module layout, the contract, the conformance suite, the test expectations and the documentation it must carry.
why: There are now a dozen signers across four modules, and the pattern is learned by reading three of them. The next contributor either reads them or guesses, and the parts that are easy to get wrong — typed-nil clients, context handling, never logging a secret — are exactly the ones a guide would catch.
criteria: Covers module layout, `go.mod` placement and the adapters CI job.
States the `Signer` contract explicitly and points at the conformance suite.
Covers the recurring traps, each with the existing adapter that demonstrates the fix.
States the evidence an adapter must carry in `docs/signers.md`.
guidance: Cite the real examples: `gcpkms`'s typed-nil check exists because that bug happened.
Coordinate with the conformance-suite issue; the guide should point at a check, not a checklist.
Be clear that an untested hardware claim is not acceptable, as `docs/signers.md` already requires.

title: feat(signers): cache a signer's address lookup
description: Let a signer whose `Address()` requires a remote call cache the result, with the cache's lifetime and invalidation explicit.
why: `Address()` is called on every signing path and for every node of a delegate tree. For a KMS signer that resolves a key to a public key remotely, that is a network round trip per node — turning a tree walk into a sequence of API calls.
criteria: A documented caching wrapper, with lifetime and invalidation stated.
A rotation that changes the address invalidates the cache, or the wrapper documents that it cannot detect one and refuses to cache across it.
Concurrency-safe, with a `-race` test.
A test proving the underlying lookup happens once for a multi-node tree.
guidance: `Address()` returning a stale value would write signatures to the wrong node — the invalidation story must be stated, not assumed.
Coordinate with the key-rotation issue so there is one notion of when an address can change.
A wrapper, not a change to the interface: not every signer needs this.

title: feat(signers): zero key material after use where the language allows
description: Audit where seeds and private keys are held in memory, zero them when their lifetime ends, and document honestly what Go cannot guarantee.
why: `NewEd25519Signer` takes a `keypair.Full` and the CLI reads a seed from the environment. Those bytes stay in memory, and Go's garbage collector may copy them. The limits here are real, and the honest statement of them is itself the deliverable.
criteria: An audit naming every place key material is held, from reading the code.
Zeroing where the library owns the buffer, with a test asserting it.
A documented statement of what Go cannot guarantee — GC copies, swap, core dumps — without overclaiming.
The CLI's environment-read path covered, since that is the most likely real exposure.
guidance: Do not claim memory hygiene Go cannot deliver; an overclaim here is worse than the current silence.
`keypair.Full` is the SDK's type and this library does not own its internals — say what that means for the guarantee.
The audit is the valuable half. If zeroing turns out to be mostly theatre, report that.

title: feat(signers): report a signer's capabilities
description: An optional interface letting a signer declare whether it is deterministic, interactive, remote, or supports batched presence, so callers and tests can adapt.
why: A caller cannot tell an in-memory ed25519 signer from a hardware device that will prompt a human. That difference governs whether retrying is safe, whether batching helps, and which conformance contract applies — and it is currently inferred from the constructor's name.
criteria: An optional interface with a documented, closed set of capabilities.
Every shipped signer declares its capabilities, asserted by a test over all of them.
The conformance suite uses the declaration to choose which contract to apply.
A signer that does not implement it gets documented conservative defaults.
guidance: Optional, so no existing signer breaks: a type assertion, not a change to `Signer`.
Conservative defaults: assume interactive and non-deterministic when unknown, since that is the safe direction for retries.
Coordinate with the conformance-suite and batched-presence issues so there is one vocabulary.

title: feat(signers): refuse to sign for the wrong network
description: Let a signer be pinned to a network passphrase and refuse any preimage built for another.
why: `Signer.Sign` receives the preimage, which carries the network id — so a signer can check it, and none does. A production key signing a testnet payload, or worse the reverse, is currently caught only by the submission failing.
criteria: A wrapper pinning a signer to one passphrase, refusing others with a distinct error.
The check compares the network id inside the preimage, not a caller-supplied string.
A test proving a mainnet-pinned signer refuses a testnet preimage and vice versa.
The source-account arm, which has no preimage, is handled explicitly rather than falling through.
guidance: Deriving the id from the passphrase and comparing to the preimage's is the only check that cannot be fooled by a wrong argument.
`network.ID` is the existing derivation — use it rather than hashing by hand.
This is a containment control for a production key; make the refusal unmistakable.

title: feat(integrations): publish the wasm package to a CDN-friendly layout
description: Publish the wasm artifact and its JavaScript glue so a browser page can load it from a URL without a bundler.
why: `@soroauth/wasm` publishes to npm, which assumes a build step. The browser passkey example is exactly the audience least likely to have one, and a script-tag path is the shortest route from reading the docs to running the thing.
criteria: A documented URL layout with versioned, immutable paths.
Subresource integrity hashes published alongside, so a page can pin what it loads.
A plain HTML page in the repo loading it with no build step, exercised in CI.
The published artifact replays the golden vectors, same as the npm path.
guidance: Immutable versioned URLs: a mutable `latest` for a signing library is a supply-chain risk, not a convenience.
Publish the integrity hashes and document their use, or the layout adds a risk without a mitigation.
Reuse the existing npm publishing pipeline rather than adding a second release path.

title: feat(integrations): devcontainer and Codespaces configuration
description: A devcontainer with Go, Node, Rust and `stellar-cli` at the repository's pinned versions.
why: `CONTRIBUTING.md` lists four toolchains at specific versions for the optional paths. A contributor who only wants to run the e2e suite has to install Rust 1.93.0 and stellar-cli 28.0.0 first, which is where most people stop.
criteria: Every pinned version matches the repository's pins, read from the pin files rather than duplicated.
`make`, `make vectors` and `make e2e` all work in it from a clean start.
Built in CI so it cannot rot silently.
Documented in CONTRIBUTING as an option, not as the required path.
guidance: Read the versions from `rust-toolchain.toml`, `go.mod` and the generator's `package.json`; a duplicated pin will drift.
Building it in CI is what keeps it working — an unbuilt devcontainer is worse than none.
Do not let it become the only supported environment; the local instructions stay.

title: feat(integrations): OpenTelemetry example covering the full flow
description: Extend the OpenTelemetry example from signing to the whole flow: both simulation passes, signing, submission and polling, as one trace.
why: `examples/opentelemetry` instruments signing. The interesting latency is elsewhere — the two simulation round trips and the submission poll — and the two-pass requirement is much easier to understand as a trace than as prose.
criteria: One trace spanning record pass, signing, enforcing pass, submission and polling, with spans named consistently.
The resource-fee difference between the two passes is visible as an attribute, since that is the point of the second pass.
No span attribute carries a secret, an entry or a signature; asserted by a test.
Runnable against testnet with documented configuration, and the example's README shows a real captured trace.
guidance: `rpcflow.SignAndSubmit` is the flow; instrument through `hooks.go` rather than forking it.
A real captured trace in the README is what makes this teach something.
Keep OpenTelemetry out of the root module; it stays an example dependency.

title: feat(integrations): Makefile target to run everything CI runs
description: A single target that runs locally everything CI runs, in CI's order, with the same commands.
why: `make` runs fmt, vet and test. CI additionally runs the vector drift check, the adapter modules, the parity suites, the wasm replay, prettier, cspell and the link check — so a branch can be green locally and red on push, which is how `spellcheck` got missed.
criteria: One target running every check CI runs, each with the same command CI uses.
Prerequisites it cannot satisfy are reported as skipped with the reason, never silently passed.
A check present in CI and absent from the target fails a meta-check, so the two cannot drift.
Documented in CONTRIBUTING alongside the existing `make` guidance.
guidance: The meta-check is the valuable part: without it this target drifts from CI within a month.
Skipped-with-a-reason is essential — a silent skip is exactly the failure mode being fixed.
Keep plain `make` fast; this is the thorough target, not a replacement.

title: docs: Go doc examples for diff.go
description: Runnable `Example` functions for `DiffEntries` and `EntryDiff.String`, in the style of the existing example files.
why: Every other major entry point gained doc examples in Wave 9. `DiffEntries` shipped after them and has none, so `pkg.go.dev` shows its signature with no worked use — and the payload-versus-signature distinction is exactly what an example conveys better than prose.
criteria: At least one example showing a payload change with a carried-over signature, since that is the finding the type exists for.
Output assertions use real values from a committed golden vector, not invented ones.
File-scoped constants, so the file cannot collide with another example file's identifiers.
`go test ./...` passes with the examples' output verified.
guidance: Read `inspect_example_test.go` and follow it exactly; consistency across the example files is the point.
Run the test to get the real output rather than predicting it — a guessed `// Output:` is the usual failure here.
Keep each example short enough to read on `pkg.go.dev` without scrolling.

title: docs: Go doc examples for verify.go
description: Runnable examples for `VerifyEntry` covering a verified node, an unsigned node and a `cannot_check` node.
why: The four verdicts exist precisely because collapsing them loses information, and nothing on `pkg.go.dev` shows a reader what each looks like in practice.
criteria: One example per verdict a classic account can produce, plus `cannot_check` for a contract address.
Output taken from a real run against a committed vector.
File-scoped constants to avoid identifier collisions with other example files.
The examples make clear that `cannot_check` is not a failure.
guidance: Follow the existing example files' structure.
`docs/verification-limits.md` has the framing — the examples should agree with it.
Do not construct an `invalid` case by hand-editing a vector; build it in code from a signed entry.

title: docs: Go doc examples for the risk analyzer
description: Runnable examples for the risk analyzer showing a clean entry and one that produces findings.
why: The analyzer is heuristic and its limits are documented separately. An example is where a reader learns what a finding looks like, and that an empty result is not a safety verdict.
criteria: One example with no findings and one with at least one finding.
A comment stating that no findings does not mean safe, consistent with `docs/analyzer-heuristics.md`.
Output from a real run.
File-scoped constants.
guidance: `docs/analyzer-heuristics.md` lists what the analyzer misses — do not imply more than it claims.
Build the risky entry in code so the example is self-contained.
Match the existing example files' style.

title: docs: Go doc examples for the envelope helpers
description: Runnable examples for `EnvelopeEntries` and `InspectEnvelope`.
why: Envelope support shipped in Wave 9 and is the entry point for anyone starting from a transaction rather than a bare entry — which is the common case, since that is what simulation returns.
criteria: An example reading entries out of an envelope and reporting their operation and entry indices.
An example covering a fee-bump envelope, since reading through to the inner transaction is the surprising part.
Output from a real run against a committed fixture.
File-scoped constants.
guidance: `envelope_test.go` has fixtures already — reuse rather than building new ones.
The index reporting is what callers need in order to put a signed entry back; make that visible.
Follow the existing example files.

title: docs: document the exported constants in one place
description: A doc.go section listing the exported constants — credential type names, verdicts, decode limits, signature shapes — with what each is for.
why: These are the values a caller switches on, and they are declared across five files. `pkg.go.dev` lists them alphabetically with no indication of which belong together.
criteria: Every exported constant covered, verified by comparing against the package's actual exported surface rather than by reading.
Grouped by the type or decision each belongs to.
States which are stable strings safe to persist and which are not.
No constant's existing doc comment is removed.
guidance: Generate the list from `go doc` output so none is missed.
`doc.go` already holds the credential-arm table; extend that rather than starting a new document.
Saying which strings are safe to persist is the genuinely useful part.

title: docs: note the fail-closed tie-break rule in CONTRIBUTING
description: State the fail-closed rule explicitly in CONTRIBUTING, with examples of where it was applied.
why: The rule governs every ambiguous decision in the codebase and lives in the project's own instructions rather than in the contributor-facing documentation. A contributor hitting an ambiguity has no way to know what the project expects.
criteria: States the rule: where the protocol or intent is ambiguous, refuse and return an error rather than guess.
Cites at least three real applications in the code, with the file.
States that the chosen reading goes in the commit message.
Placed near 'What a change needs', which already carries the related rules.
guidance: The target-address rule and the re-sign refusal are the clearest examples — both already have doc comments explaining the reasoning.
Keep it short; it belongs beside the existing rules, not as a new top-level section.
Do not restate what 'What a change needs' already says.

title: docs: add the diff subcommand to the CLI docs index
description: Audit the CLI documentation for subcommands added after it was written and add the missing ones consistently.
why: `diff` has a README section; whether every subcommand is represented consistently across the README, the docs index and the man page is unverified, and an undocumented subcommand is effectively absent.
criteria: A list, from the dispatcher rather than from the documentation, of every subcommand.
Each present in the README's CLI section and the docs index, or an explicit note of why not.
Any gap found is fixed in the same style as the surrounding entries.
The PR reports which were missing.
guidance: Read the dispatch switch in `cmd/soroauth/main.go` for the authoritative list; the documentation is what is being checked.
`commandSpecs` is checked against the usage text by a test — the README is the uncovered copy.
If everything is already consistent, say so; that is a valid result.

title: docs: state the Go version policy in the README
description: Say in the README which Go versions are supported, and that the floor moves only when a dependency raises it.
why: `go.mod` declares a floor and `CONTRIBUTING.md` mentions it in passing. Someone deciding whether the library fits their build reads the README, where the answer is absent.
criteria: The supported floor stated, read from `go.mod` rather than from memory.
The policy stated: the floor moves only when a dependency forces it.
Consistent with `docs/sdk-support.md`, which governs the dependency pin.
Placed in the install section where a reader will be looking.
guidance: Read the version from `go.mod` and quote it; a stale version number here is worse than none.
`docs/sdk-support.md` already has the pin policy — link rather than restate.
One short paragraph.

title: docs: a worked example in the DiffEntries doc comment
description: Add a short worked example to `DiffEntries`'s doc comment showing the stale-signature case as a table.
why: `ExpirationAfter` has a worked table in its doc comment and it is the clearest explanation of the inclusive bound anywhere in the repo. The payload-versus-signature distinction would benefit from the same treatment.
criteria: A table showing which field changed, whether the payload moved, and whether a carried-over signature is stale.
Covers the four combinations: identical, signature only, payload only, both.
Consistent with what the code actually produces, checked by running it.
Adds no claim not already true of the implementation.
guidance: `ExpirationAfter`'s doc comment is the model for the format.
Run the four cases and transcribe the real summaries rather than paraphrasing them.
Keep it compact; the doc comment is already long.

title: docs: explain the deterministic key labels in the glossary
description: Add the deterministic test-key scheme to the glossary, with a pointer to the fuller explanation.
why: Test keys derived from `sha256(label)` appear throughout the vectors, the fixtures and the e2e suite. A reader meeting `soroauth-vector-signer-1` in a vector has no entry point for what it means.
criteria: A glossary entry explaining the derivation and why it is deterministic.
States plainly that these are public test keys that must never be funded on mainnet.
Links the existing fuller document rather than restating it.
Fits the glossary's existing grouping and tone.
guidance: Wave 9 documented the scheme in one place — find it and link it.
The mainnet warning is the part that matters; keep it prominent.
`docs/glossary.md` groups terms by what they belong to, not alphabetically — place it accordingly.

title: docs: add diff and verify to the glossary
description: Add glossary entries for the project's own terms introduced since it was written: stale signature, payload change, credential-node path, verdict.
why: The glossary has a section for this project's own vocabulary. `DiffEntries` introduced four more terms that appear in output a user reads, and none is defined anywhere a reader would look.
criteria: Entries for stale signature, payload change, node path and verdict.
Each says plainly that it is this project's term and not protocol vocabulary.
Cross-linked with the existing entries that relate to them.
Placed in the existing 'this project's own terms' section.
guidance: The glossary is explicit about which terms are the project's own — keep that distinction.
Define them as the code uses them; read `diff.go` and `verify.go` rather than inferring.
Match the existing entries' length and tone.

title: docs: link the e2e results from the scenario table
description: Cross-link `e2e/README.md`'s scenario table with the corresponding runs in `e2e/RESULTS.md`.
why: One document says what each scenario proves and the other records that it ran, with no link between them. A reader checking whether a claim is backed by a real run has to match them up by hand.
criteria: Each scenario in the table links its recorded result.
A scenario with no recorded run is marked as such rather than left ambiguous.
Links verified by the link checker.
No claim is added about a scenario that has not run.
guidance: `RESULTS.md` is committed only from a real run — do not add a placeholder for a scenario that has not been run.
`RESULTS.md` is in `.prettierignore`; take care not to reformat it.
If a scenario has no run, say so plainly; that is useful information.

title: docs: state what the fuzz targets assert
description: Extend `docs/fuzzing.md` with a per-target statement of what each target asserts, beyond not crashing.
why: The document covers how to run the fuzzers and how a crash becomes a regression seed. It does not say what each target checks, so a reader cannot tell which are real property checks and which only test for panics — a difference that decides how much the suite proves.
criteria: One line per target naming its invariants, read from the target's source.
Targets that only check for panics are identified as such, honestly.
The list is complete against the targets that exist, verified by enumerating them.
Fits the document's existing structure.
guidance: Read each target rather than inferring from its name.
Being honest that a target only checks for panics is the useful part; it identifies where to strengthen.
The document already names six targets — check whether that count is still right.

title: docs: README section on what soroauth deliberately does not do
description: A short README section listing the non-goals, so a reader can rule the library in or out quickly.
why: The non-goals are real and deliberate — no transaction builder, no key manager, no interpretation of what a call does — and they are scattered across doc comments. A reader evaluating the library discovers them by not finding the feature.
criteria: Lists the non-goals with one line each on why, and where to look instead.
Points at `soroauth-explain` for interpretation and at the SDK's `txnbuild` for transaction building.
Placed before the status section, where a reader deciding will reach it.
Claims nothing about another project that is not true today.
guidance: These are design decisions, not gaps — the tone should reflect that.
Check what `soroauth-explain` actually does before describing it.
Keep it to a short list; this is a filter, not an essay.

title: docs: fix the stale adapter count in the signers guide
description: Audit `docs/signers.md` against the adapters and signers that now exist, and correct anything stale.
why: Signers were added across the wave and the guide was written partway through. A guide that omits a shipped signer sends a reader to write their own, which is the specific outcome the guide exists to prevent.
criteria: Every signer in the root package and every adapter module represented.
The evidence column accurate for each — what is proven by test, by vector, by e2e, or only by hand.
Any signer whose evidence was overstated is corrected, and the PR says which.
No signer is claimed to be hardware-tested without a recorded run.
guidance: Enumerate from the code and the `adapters/` directory, not from the guide.
The evidence column is the guide's most valuable part; accuracy there matters more than completeness of prose.
An overstatement found here is worth its own commit noting what was wrong.

title: docs: add a short security note about hostile entries
description: Note in `SECURITY.md` that entries come from elsewhere and state what the library does to bound that, with pointers.
why: `SECURITY.md` covers reporting and the unaudited status. The most common real exposure — decoding an entry supplied by someone else — is handled in the code and not mentioned where a security reader looks.
criteria: States that entries are untrusted input and names the bound that applies.
Points at the decode limits and the adversarial corpus.
Does not overclaim: says what is bounded and what a caller still must do.
Consistent with the threat model document if that exists, and flagged for reconciliation if not.
guidance: `decode.go` states the reasoning; cite it rather than restating it.
Keep it to a paragraph pointing at the real material.
Do not weaken the existing unaudited statement.

title: docs: date and version every evidence claim in the README
description: Audit the README's evidence claims — the SDK pin, the protocol version, the testnet results, the CAP-85 finding — and give each a date or version.
why: The README states facts that were true when checked: testnet's protocol version, the SDK's contents, that no CAP-85 change is needed. Without a date each reads as current indefinitely, which for a protocol-tracking library is how documentation becomes wrong.
criteria: Every evidence claim carries the date or version it was checked at.
Any claim that cannot be dated is re-verified and dated, or removed.
The CAP-85 section states the SDK version its finding applies to.
No claim's substance changes without the re-verification recorded in the PR.
guidance: The repo's evidence rule applies to the audit too: re-verify rather than copying a date from a commit message.
If a claim turns out stale, that is its own commit stating what was wrong and how you found it.
Dating a claim is not hedging; it is what makes it checkable.

title: docs: a one-page summary of the signing flow
description: A single page showing the path from unsigned entry to submitted transaction, pointing at the function responsible for each step.
why: `ARCHITECTURE.md` maps files to responsibilities and the README explains the two-pass requirement. Nothing shows the sequence on one page, which is what a newcomer needs before either document is readable.
criteria: The full sequence: simulate, choose arm, build preimage, hash, sign, write, re-simulate, assemble, submit.
Each step names the function that does it, verified against the code.
Fits on one page and links the deeper documents.
Uses the existing rendered diagrams if they already cover it, rather than adding a near-duplicate.
guidance: Check `docs/diagrams/` first — this may be a short page linking an existing diagram rather than new artwork.
Naming the responsible function is what makes it navigable; verify each against the source.
Do not restate the two-pass explanation; link it.

title: chore: add the workflow's own path to every paths filter
description: Audit every workflow with a `paths:` filter and confirm each lists its own file, adding it where missing.
why: Four workflows were fixed for this, which means the rule exists and nothing enforces it. A workflow added later with a `paths:` filter and no self-reference cannot validate its own edits — exactly how a new job once reached main unexecuted.
criteria: Every `paths:`-filtered workflow lists its own path.
A check or test that fails when one does not, so the rule holds without vigilance.
The PR reports which workflows were missing it.
CONTRIBUTING's 'Editing a workflow' section is accurate afterwards.
guidance: CONTRIBUTING's 'Editing a workflow' section explains why; this makes it enforced rather than advisory.
A small script or Go test over the workflow files is enough — no new CI job, given the check-count cap.
If every workflow already complies, ship the check anyway; that is the deliverable.

title: chore: a make target that lists every check with its command
description: Extend `make help` to list every check the project runs and the exact command for each.
why: `make help` lists the Makefile's targets. Several checks CI runs are not targets — prettier, cspell, the link check — so the help output is not a complete answer to 'what do I need to pass'.
criteria: Lists every check with its command, including those not wrapped by a target.
Says which gate a merge and which are advisory.
Generated from one source, so a new check appears without a second edit.
The output fits a terminal screen.
guidance: Coordinate with the run-everything-CI-runs target so there is one list, not two.
Distinguishing required from advisory is the useful part — the repo caps PR checks at three for a reason.
Keep it readable: a wall of text is not help.

title: chore: .gitignore entries for the generated build outputs
description: Audit `.gitignore` against what the build and test targets actually produce, and add anything missing.
why: The build produces `bin/`, wasm output, a parity venv, Rust `target/` and a tools directory. Anything missing from `.gitignore` shows up as untracked noise, and untracked noise is how a generated artifact gets committed by accident.
criteria: A clean checkout stays clean after `make`, `make wasm`, `make parity` and `make e2e`.
`git status` is empty after each, demonstrated in the PR.
Nothing currently tracked is newly ignored.
`node_modules` and every tool cache covered.
guidance: Run each target and read `git status`; do not reason about what they might produce.
Check `cspell.json`'s `ignorePaths` for a list of generated directories as a starting point.
Take care not to ignore a committed generated artifact such as the vectors or the fuzz corpora.

title: chore: make the e2e suite report its skip reasons
description: Make every skip in the e2e suite state why, so a passing run with no scenarios is distinguishable from a real pass.
why: The suite needs a reachable RPC, friendbot and a built contract. A missing prerequisite that produces a silent skip makes the suite report success for doing nothing, which is the worst possible outcome for the only tests that touch a real network.
criteria: Every skip names the missing prerequisite.
A summary line reports how many scenarios ran and how many skipped.
A run where everything skipped is not reported as a pass.
`e2e/README.md` states the prerequisites the suite checks.
guidance: `golden_test.go` fails rather than skipping when it finds no vectors — the same reasoning applies here.
The count summary is what makes a silent skip visible in CI logs.
A skip is legitimate; a silent one is not.

title: chore: add a dependabot group for the adapter modules
description: Group the adapter modules' dependency updates so cloud SDK bumps arrive as one pull request per module rather than several.
why: There are three adapter modules each depending on a large cloud SDK. Ungrouped, a single SDK release produces a run of near-identical pull requests, and a wave of those is how an auto-merging bot broke main twice.
criteria: Updates grouped per module, with the grouping documented in the config.
The pinned reference SDK's existing ignore rules are unchanged.
